    "square describes a broader and more varied course catalog (extensive AP plus vocational/trade offerings) than circle": "Square repeatedly claims strong advanced and vocational programming: “Aloha has the best AP classes... offers the most AP classes of any in the state” and notes “unusual classes outside academics like woodworking, art, and automotive” plus an international-traveling automotive team; circle's reviews praise teachers and general academics but do not report similar extensive AP or vocational program breadth.",
    
    "circle reports stronger staff development, collaboration, and administrative support for teachers than square": "Circle reviews state institutional staff support: “There are so many opportunities for staff development and for teachers to collaborate with administration,” “Falcon staff hold each other accountable,” and “This school is student centered and so supportive of it's staff.” Square instead documents administrative disengagement: “this is where the gaslighting begins,” “they are excellent listeners... then the ghosting begins,” indicating far less perceived administrative support.",

  "circle highlights exceptionally supportive band and flute teachers and unusual teacher outreach more than square": "Circle gives concrete positive examples of extracurricular teacher engagement—“Her band teacher not only supported her to go to state competition, he went with her!!!!” and “the flute teacher offered to do private lessons with my child in the summer and come to the home!!!” —a level of individual outreach absent from Square.",

["{

["{

["{

  "square exhibits stronger socioeconomic and parent/student clique exclusion than circle": "Square repeatedly notes social stratification and favoritism: \"many of the students here come from wealthy families, and they act as if they are better,\" \"a big clique between parents,\" and \"a select, 'elite' group of students that are very much favorited by the principals,\" while circle does not report entrenched parent cliques or wealth-based student exclusion.",

  "circle reports staff immaturity and unprofessional conduct interfering with learning more than square": "Circle explicitly states \"a portion of the staff are just immature and unprofessional, and it gets in the way of learning sometimes,\" a clear claim about staff behavior impacting instruction that square does not frame in the same way (square includes mixed statements like 'kind, caring' staff and separate complaints about unengaged teachers, but not 'immature' staff).",

["{
  "circle reports stronger career and technical programs, competitive teams and student leadership opportunities than square": "Circle explicitly praises “career and technical education programs (Agriculture, FACS and Business) are some of the best in the state,” notes that “4N6 teams consistently have state qualifiers and placers,” and says the school “provide[s] multiple opportunities for students to be involved in leadership on the local, state and national levels,” while Square’s entries do not describe comparable CTE programs, statewide competitions, or leadership pipelines.",

  "circle reports severe ethnic-based bullying and administrative failure (legal threat) more than square": "Circle describes a case where a child was “the only Hispanic child in the school and they would not deal with the blatant bullying,” and the parent says “I even had to threaten a lawsuit,” indicating an alleged ethnic-targeted bullying incident and perceived administrative inaction; Square mentions being “called 'stupid' because we moved here” and “different rules for new kids,” but does not describe the same explicit ethnic-targeted incident or a parental legal threat.",
  "square emphasizes literacy, graduation outcomes and community satisfaction more than circle": "Square’s positive review asserts “the primary concern is to teach and graduate literate students” and multiple parents report being “happy with the school and proud that [our] kids go to school there,” while Circle focuses its praise on technical programs, fine arts, and extracurricular accomplishments rather than claiming a strong community-wide emphasis on literacy/graduation.",
  "square reports a perceived prioritization of dress code/appearance enforcement over academic focus more than circle": "Square complains “Jacksonville high school cares more about what their students are wearing than what their learning,” indicating a belief that school priorities favor uniform/dress enforcement over instruction; Circle contains no comparable claim about dress code priorities.",
  "square contains more reports of parents immediately removing children or switching to homeschool than circle": "Square includes “We took one 15 year old daughter out and put in home school” and “I'm getting my kids out of this district ASAP,” showing parents withdrawing students, whereas Circle reports a long-term family requesting a transfer after 13 years but not the same immediate homeschool/withdrawal behavior."
}"]

["{
  "square contains an active, racially charged mascot controversy and staff racial/insensitivity incidents that circle does not": "Square explicitly documents a mascot dispute and staff comments: “Anderson High School has become an incredibly divisive atmosphere because of the school mascot issue,” and a coach who says “we need to get over slavery,” and who derides Islam; Circle contains no comparable reports of racial/insensitive controversies.",
  "square reports bullying incidents and ineffective school response while circle does not": "Square states a failure to protect students and ignoring complaints: “My sister was bullied throughout her time there and the school did nothing to help her,” and an assistant principal who “simply ignored me”; Circle only mentions general \"drama\" and not systemic unresolved bullying.",
  "circle has fewer and narrower extracurricular options than square": "Circle says “If a student is not interested in sports then there are very few extra-curricular activities to choose from,” whereas Square repeatedly lists many programs and clubs and claims it is “virtually impossible not to fit in” and that the daughter found clubs that helped her succeed.",
  "circle has more limited academic course breadth and rigid college/non-college tracking than square": "Circle describes constrained academic pathways: “students are basicly put on one of two paths; college bound or not worth anyone's time” and “very easy to take almost every college prep class in four years,” while Square highlights varied student outcomes, high test scores, and opportunities for students to improve academically through other programs rather than describing rigid tracking.",
  "square enforces punitive fee policies and shows administrative unresponsiveness that circle does not report": "Square recounts fees blocking graduation and ignored appeals: “they gave in to a bullying mob” (context of administration failing) and “fees over 300... without paying them my brother would not be able to graduate” and an assistant principal “simply ignored me”; Circle includes no reports of fees withheld or unresponsive administration.",
  "circle describes a safer, small-town physical environment while square emphasizes social division and conflict": "Circle explicitly calls the community “a very safe place and the town is beautiful,” whereas Square emphasizes a “divisive atmosphere” tied to mascot fights and interpersonal conflict that leaves “the kids... caught in the middle.”",
  "circle reports a visible youth drinking culture in the community that square does not": "Circle states a common weekend activity: “for most students the favorite weekend activity is drinking,” a community behavior not described in Square.",
  "circle portrays more consistently positive teacher performance while square reports mixed teacher quality": "Circle asserts teachers are generally good: “the teachers are typically very good at teaching” and “the teachers are really great,” while Square contains conflicting teacher reports: “there were some excellent teachers, but unfortunately also quite a few who did not seem to enjoy educating young people.”",
  "square provides more varied, inclusive pathways (clubs/programs) that enabled academic and social turnaround compared with circle": "Square gives specific outcomes tied to extracurricular fit: “My daughter went from failing to success in one year both socially and academically because she could join some clubs that fit her” and calls out “so many programs and clubs for the students to participate in,” whereas Circle emphasizes limited extracurricular options and fewer pathways for nonathletic or divergent students."
}"]

["{
  "circle exhibits systematic deprioritization of arts/theater programming while square does not report such problems": "Circle states explicitly that \"South Summit offers no drama classes\" and that the school's \"theater and even a 'Drama Room' but neither are used to teach drama,\" and notes that any drama instruction is relegated to limited after‑school meetings; Square simply offers blanket praise and includes no comparable report of missing arts instruction.",

["{
  "square reports chronic teacher and principal turnover more than circle": "Square states explicitly that \"teachers being let go constantly and the principal always being someone new every year,\" describing repeated staff and leadership churn that is not described with the same specificity in Circle (Circle mentions poor administration but does not detail constant turnover).",

  "circle reports stronger teacher and counselor hands-on support for students than square": "Circle asserts \"Every staff member will go out of their way to help the students\" and that \"The counselors were always willing to work with you,\" whereas Square blames the environment and staff instability for worsening student experience and provides no examples of staff proactively supporting students.",
  "square reports negative impact on student mental health and leaving to alternative graduation routes more than circle": "Square explains the reviewer’s \"mental health was declining in this environment\" and that they \"left and graduated online,\" indicating the school environment contributed to withdrawal and remote completion; Circle, by contrast, describes successful college transitions and does not report the same mental-health-driven departure.",

["{
  "circle shows more administrative instability, poor communication with parents, and organizational chaos than square": "Circle repeatedly describes leadership turnover, missing or absent principals, last-minute staffing and campus moves, and broken promises to parents: e.g. “The principal spends all her time in her office… Parents have no been involved… A parent letter was sent home saying that there would be meetings but not one has taken place,” and “they moved her in the middle of the school semester… one of the teachers messed up the class schedules.” Square contains no complaints about leadership or chaotic operations; it instead highlights a stable program (IB) that families embrace.",

  "circle reports more disciplinary problems and erosion of school culture and safety than square": "Circle recounts fights, students taking advantage of lax discipline, and a loss of the prior school culture after administrative change: “Ppl are fighting because they know they can get away with it… This year, since the new principal came… parents and students wait a very long time to address issues,” and “We have lost our fun activities…the students would seem excited about coming to school” under previous leadership.   "square features university-linked Career and Technical Education partnerships whereas circle emphasizes traditional extracurricular programs like agriculture, basketball, and art": "Square highlights a regional Career and Technical Education Center with \"an industrial engineering program that has been designed with Texas A&M University,\" showing formal higher-education partnership and vocational pathways; Circle instead emphasizes \"involvement in basketball, agriculture, art, and other extra curricular activities\" with no mention of university-linked CTE programs.",
  "square offers advanced academic pathways but signals uneven implementation and persistently low standardized scores, while circle credits steady teacher-led preparation for college success": "Square admits \"Low act and SAT score\" and warns the \"International Baccalaureate Programme is still too new; stick with AP classes,\" reflecting uneven advanced-program implementation and weak test outcomes despite AP/IB availability; Circle asserts \"The teachers/ instruction I earned from Valley Springs prepared me for my post secondary level education\" and chronicles the reviewer completing undergraduate and graduate degrees, indicating consistent college readiness attributed to instruction.",

["{
  "circle emphasizes a Christian faith–centered mission and explicit religious formation far more than square": "Circle repeatedly foregrounds religion and faith formation: phrases like “Christ on and off campus,” “Christ-centered,” “teach the Word of God,” retreat conversions (student ‘accepted Jesus Christ as her Lord and Savior’), daily prayers, and mission trips to Zambia indicate institutional integration of Christian doctrine that is absent from Square.",
  "circle reports more extensive alumni success, multi‑generation families, and long term community ties than square": "Circle contains many specific accounts of long relationships and outcomes—multiple families with children/grandchildren spanning decades, alumni who became doctors, ROTC grads, missionaries, and college‑prepared graduates—whereas Square gives only brief student perspective on AP/honors preparing for college and no multi‑generational/alumni narrative.",
  "circle documents operational strains (teacher turnover, financial stress, and aging or inadequate facilities) more than square": "Circle reviews explicitly mention “Very high teacher turnover,” being “barely able to pay bills,” facilities ‘wanting,’ and mobile classrooms in one passage: “Middle School is in mobile units,” while Square provides no comparable complaints about finances, turnover, or facility decline.",
  "circle describes more active parent involvement and open access to staff and administration than square": "Multiple Circle reviewers stress parental engagement and that “parents are encouraged to be involved,” “open door policy,” teachers making themselves available for meetings/tutoring, and administrators listening to parents; Square does not report this pattern of structured parent engagement.",
  "circle reports a strong emphasis on character, discipline, and behavioral expectations tied to school values more than square": "Circle repeatedly notes discipline and moral standards—expectation to ‘live a life that exemplifies Christ,’ administrators backing teachers on discipline, praise for a disciplined environment—whereas Square makes no claims about explicit discipline policies or values-based behavioral enforcement.",
  "square presents a large school environment and identity as a big high school more than circle": "Square opens by stating “It is a big school.   "square highlights strong honors/AP academic preparation and perceived college readiness more explicitly than circle": "Square reviewer emphasizes being “enrolled in all honors/AP courses” and that Garnet Valley “prepares (especially AP and honors) students so that they feel prepared when they reach college,” while Circle mentions college preparation but focuses more broadly on spiritual formation, extracurriculars, and alumni outcomes rather than a specific AP/honors program.",

  "circle lists a broader and more varied set of extracurricular and support programs (tutoring, counseling, LIPS, music, missions, athletics) than square": "Circle enumerates many programs and supports—after‑school tutoring, LIPS, counseling, private music lessons, sports, dance, mission trips, and retreats—whereas Square mentions only general services for disabilities and no comparable variety of extracurricular or specialized support offerings.",
  "circle shows a pronounced connection to military families and frequent relocation effects more than square": "Circle repeatedly notes military family dynamics—‘associated with the military,’ recommendations to military friends, and staff/families moving with deployments—framing school practices around transience; Square contains no similar references to military community or mobility.",
  "circle contains both praise for staff accessibility and counterclaims of administrative unresponsiveness/financial motive whereas square primarily offers unambiguous praise for staff and district support": "Circle includes many reviewers praising teachers being available and supportive but also multiple criticisms—‘administration is lacking,’ ‘school only concern is money’—reflecting mixed reports about leadership; Square’s remarks are uniformly positive about teachers and district services with no such administrative criticism."
}"]

    "circle reports more unresolved bullying and racism incidents than square": "Circle states racist remarks go unaddressed and bullying persisted: “Racist remarks are obviously heard and NOT DEALT with” and “My son was targeted and bullied for two weeks and they never did anything about it,” whereas Square mentions aggressive, racist student behavior (e.g., throwing items and calling a substitute racist) but frames it as behavior by some rowdy students within an otherwise improving, supportive school.",

    "square shows more evidence of supportive administration and schoolwide student engagement programs than circle": "Square repeatedly highlights proactive administration and programs: “Child centered school with caring educators and administrators,” “There are incentives in place and opportunities for all,” and “Administration is caring and supportive of students, faculty, and staff,” while Circle describes administrative hostility and inconsistent support except for counseling.",
    "circle shows more social exclusion and newcomer discomfort than square": "Circle notes peer cliques and uncomfortable majority demographics: “The kids are very reluctant to acknowledge anyone they havent known since they were small” and stepping into the school “sure was uncomfortable,” whereas Square emphasizes diversity and staff efforts to know students personally: “It has much diversity” and “Current administration ... makes an effort to get to know students on a personal level.”",

["{
  "circle enforces stricter graduation requirements and academic rigor than square": "Circle explicitly cites requirements that increase rigor and graduation difficulty — “they do require a senior project that is too stressful to graduate and computer apps is also required” and repeatedly praises “high standards” and preparing students for “the rigors of college life,” whereas Square includes multiple complaints that “all of them make class far too easy” and “It requires very little work,” showing weaker perceived rigor.",
  "square reports overcrowded classrooms and large class sizes more than circle": "Square repeatedly describes space/enrollment problems that hinder learning: “most classes are overcrowded,” “classes are so large I'm being held back by other students,” while Circle offers no comparable statements about overcrowding or large class sizes.",
  "square reports pervasive homophobic harassment and bullying problems more than circle": "Square states a daily hostile climate around sexuality — “can't go a single day without hearing a crack about homosexuality” and notes “a lot of bullying and not enough help,” whereas Circle does not describe pervasive harassment and instead rhetorically questions a bullying claim, suggesting the school blames students or parents rather than acknowledging systemic harassment.",
  "square reports student drug use and inappropriate on-campus conduct more than circle": "Square specifically calls out behavioral issues beyond bullying: “There are many students who associate with drugs and innapropriate conduct within the school's walls,” a problem absent from Circle's descriptions.",
  "square lists multiple explicit external academic partnerships and dual-enrollment options more than circle": "Square details concrete program partnerships and alternatives: “dual-enrollment program,” “AP classes supported by VASS,” “BRVGS,” “partnership with Reynolds Community College,” and “in-house virtual Governor's school option,” while Circle only generically mentions “Many options, and very comprehensive education” without naming external partners.",
  "circle emphasizes alumni success and strong community/school pride more than square": "Circle foregrounds long-term outcomes and local pride: “I know of hundreds of successful adults that came out of this district,” “Jersey Shore Bulldogs rock the house,” and statements like “If I had children I would gladly send them,” whereas Square's positive comments focus more on specific programs and supports rather than alumni success.",
  "square reports perceived favoritism toward affluent students more than circle": "Square contains an explicit claim of unequal treatment by class: “as a student who is upper middle class I feel like the school only favors to rich people and people who have no disabilities,” a direct accusation of socioeconomic favoritism not made in Circle, which instead attributes low achievement to parental neglect.",

}"]

  "square describes more staff and administrative engagement and personalized attention than circle": "Square states \"teacher support, principal is approachable, involved and friendly\" and that \"staff and faculty get to know each child,\" while Circle only offers a generic \"The teachers are always a help\" without mention of administrative involvement or personalized staff attention.",
  "square reports school safety and lack of bullying whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly says the student \"feels safe and not bullied,\" providing a claim about school safety; Circle contains no statement about safety, bullying, or disciplinary climate.",
  "square indicates a smaller school and community environment that gives students more individual opportunity than circle": "Square repeatedly emphasizes size and community: \"we are in this smaller school district,\" \"PASD is small enough that every kid has a chance to shine,\" and \"great community involvement,\" while Circle does not reference school size or community structure.",
  "square documents robust extracurricular offerings and school spirit whereas circle does not": "Square lists \"lots of school spirit, and great clubs\" as concrete features of student life; Circle does not describe clubs, spirit, or extracurricular programming.",
  "circle reports visible recent improvement and institutional progress more than square": "Circle opens with \"This school has came a long way!!!\" and emphasizes ongoing growth, a theme of recent improvement not stated in Square's reviews.",
  "circle highlights student physical development more than square": "Circle explicitly mentions students \"growing academically and physically,\" a focus on physical growth or development not present in Square's text.",
  "square includes at least one report of significant interpersonal conflict with students, staff, or administration that circle does not": "Square contains a contradictory but specific negative report—\"I did not even think I was going to be able to make it to graduation because of the things I had to deal with by students, staff and admin\"—indicating an account of serious interpersonal problems absent from Circle."
}"]

  "circle reports harsher, demeaning teacher communication with students and parents more than square": "Circle reports multiple complaints about how staff speak to families: \"teachers talk... in an harsh manner and instead of instructing a child to do something, they tend to 'bark' it at them\" and \"numerous teachers talk to the parents the same way,\" while Square praises teachers doing their best and gives no examples of demeaning communication.",
  "square offers and credits a formal advanced academic program (IB) and stronger academic outcomes more than circle": "Square repeatedly describes an International Baccalaureate program and its results: \"As an IB student...the IB students enjoy their courses and make excellent grades\" and cites academic wins like the academic challenge team, while Circle complains \"test scores are so down\" and describes the school as \"mediocre at best boasting only a grade of C.\"",
  "square reports effective administrative leadership improving safety and student behavior more than circle": "Square attributes concrete climate improvement to new leadership: \"Since the new principle came in, behavior and illegal substance usage has drastically improved\" and notes fights have stopped, whereas Circle contains statements of insecurity and disorder: \"Deplorable.   "circle shows greater variability in individual teacher relationships (some named praised, others criticized) than square": "Circle contains juxtaposed individual teacher praise and broad staff criticism—parents name and praise specific teachers (\"I love Mrs M Jackson...Mrs Amodei Mrs Edwards\") alongside complaints about how many teachers behave—whereas Square frames contrasts at the program level (IB vs traditional) rather than naming widely variable individual teacher relationships."

  "square reports more bullying, peer pressure, and inconsistent handling of behavioral issues than circle": "Square contains multiple negative safety/climate reports — “There is a lot of peer pressure, bullying and not a lot of self respect... some teachers have very poor boundaries... administration would ignore the situations” — while Circle offers no accounts of bullying or safety problems.",
  "circle reports poorer college preparedness and attributes it to teacher quality more than square": "Circle states the reviewer felt “not adaquately preparded for higher education and felt behind many of the other students once I began college” and blames “many teachers I didn't feel were up to standard,” a specific outcome-related criticism not asserted in Square (which instead emphasizes college-prep programs and rigorous projects).",

["{
  "circle emphasizes overcrowding and calls for new facilities more than square": "Circle opens with an explicit facilities complaint: “we need to make a new high school becasue we are over crowded!” while Square only contains a limited note about class size in context of poor teaching: “Poor teaching skills + large class sizes = really bad problems,” so Circle frames crowding as a primary, district-level infrastructure issue rather than an occasional class-size complaint.",
  "square describes a broader array of academic and extracurricular programs and college-prep supports more than circle": "Square lists many concrete programs and academic offerings: “personal planning workshops, college rep visits, career panel presentations, ROP classes, 17 AP classes, Math Academy, Excel schedule… choir, the band, the theater, ceramics, yoga, Link Crew, the counseling office,” and cites outcomes: “Graduates of SCHS are ready for college and career” and students going to “prestigious schools,” whereas Circle mentions only a few programs and focuses on decline rather than breadth.",
  "circle reports district-level leadership and communication failures more than square": "Circle directly blames leadership and district communication: “school leadership not being effective,” “The superintendent is not very well equipped to improve the school,” and “The school district needs to communicate its needs and work more with the community,” whereas Square contains praise for administration (“The administration is kind and welcoming”) and no sustained critique of district leadership or communication.",
  "circle highlights decline of specific extracurricular programs (music and wrestling) more than square": "Circle names program-level declines as specific trends: “The music programs used to be excellent but have also declined in recent years” and “the Wrestling program used to be excellent and has also declined,” while Square describes arts and athletics as active strengths (e.g., “SCHIS is rich in arts, athletics and academics”) and does not document such program decline.",
  "square shows greater variability in teacher quality including reports of unresponsive or overwhelmed teachers causing students to leave more than circle": "Square contains both praise and serious criticism of staff: one reviewer calls staff “dedicated,” another says there are “too many broken, uninspired and disconnected teachers,” and an account states teachers were “too busy to help… My daughter withdrew from SCHS and went to another school,” whereas Circle’s comments about staff are uniformly that “Most teachers/staff are good and care about their students” with no comparable report of overwhelmed teachers driving student exits.",
  "circle criticizes a community overemphasis on sports and name-playing more than square": "Circle states a community-level cultural problem: “The community focuses too much on sports and there is a lot of 'name-playing,'” a critique absent from Square, which instead lists athletic programs as positive offerings without describing community over-prioritization of sports.",
  "square emphasizes student diversity and active celebration of diversity more than circle": "Square repeatedly highlights and celebrates diversity as a feature of the school: “One of the outstanding features of SCHS is the diversity of its student body: tall-short, fat-skinny, rich-poor… black, Hispanic, Asian, white, gay, straight,” and notes clubs/events that celebrate diversity, while Circle makes no mention of student racial, socioeconomic, or cultural diversity."
}"]

["{
  "square has more visible, engaged leadership and longer staff tenure than circle": "Square repeatedly names an involved principal who \"introduce[s] himself to parents, students\" and \"shows up at sporting events,\" and a reviewer states \"I've worked at this school for over 15 years,\" whereas Circle opens with \"Southern Vance has no leadership\" and reports the school board \"move a good principal for nothing,\" indicating leadership instability and weaker visible administration.",
  "square offers identifiable specialty academies and clearer college pathways while circle reports poor college placement and low expectations": "Square mentions concrete programs and outcomes—\"Academy of Justice,\" \"Environmental Innovation Academy,\" and multiple comments that children \"went on to college/career well equipped\"—whereas Circle claims coaches \"never send a child to college\" and that \"the children at this school are looked apon as people who are going to fail.\"",
  "square demonstrates stronger school spirit, multi-generational community ties, and institutional extracurricular support than circle": "Square describes \"school spirit and pride is incredible,\" \"Many generations of families have been a part of the traditions,\" and programs/athletics described as \"outstanding,\" while Circle says \"athletics at southern has no support but from the parents\" and points to lack of institutional support for extracurriculars.",
  "circle shows more teacher and coach unprofessionalism and derogatory treatment of students than square": "Circle accuses staff of immaturity—\"The teachers act more like children than the children\"—and cites a coach saying \"the players on the basketball team don't have the mental IQ to play basketball,\" whereas Square contains multiple statements that \"teachers really care,\" \"staff is supportive,\" and administrators \"show his staff appreciation.\"",
  "circle reports more pervasive student behavior problems and inconsistent discipline than square": "Circle explicitly identifies the \"biggest issue the school has is a behavior problem\" and blames inadequate correction by parents, while Square's reviews overwhelmingly describe positive climate and support (e.g., \"students are amazingly caring and considerate\") with only isolated safety claims (one reviewer alleges weapons and neighborhood crime), indicating behavior/discipline problems are more central in Circle's reviews.",
  "square reports more proactive parent communication and informational outreach than circle": "Square states the school is \"very informative with keeping parents informed on everything,\" and multiple reviewers praise staff outreach, while Circle contains no comparable claims about systematic parent communication and instead emphasizes parental responsibility for behavior and parent-led support of athletics."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports more student fighting and behavior problems tied to demographic change than square": "Circle explicitly links rising fighting and behavior to incoming students: \"students from Akron are moving into the school system and behaviour has been ridiculous\" and repeatedly states \"fighting is becoming an issue,\" whereas Square mentions bullying in passing but does not connect misconduct to demographic shifts or widespread fighting.",

  "circle shows stronger evidence of rigorous advanced coursework and higher academic expectations than square": "Circle repeatedly praises fast paced advanced classes and high expectations: \"advanced classes are fast-paced and a great challenge\" and \"High expectations for achievement and success,\" while Square contains explicit complaints that the school \"doesn't offer as many academic classes... and doesn't seem to challenge me\" despite mentioning some good test scores.",
  "square documents a university-partnered engineering program that circle does not": "Square states \"They have brought in an engineering program that links up with SDSU,\" a concrete institutional partnership and program detail that is not mentioned in Circle.",
  "circle reports active staffing and leadership investments (new hires and a dean of students) more than square": "Circle notes \"many great additions have been brought in such as new educators and dean of students\" and praises ongoing hiring, while Square emphasizes facilities and individual staff rather than schoolwide staffing or leadership hiring initiatives.",
  "square reports recent bond-funded facilities improvements more than circle": "Square specifies infrastructure investment: \"The campus has new classrooms, athletic areas and future construction projects are being paid for by two bonds that have already been passed,\" a detailed funding and facilities claim not present in Circle.",

  "square contains named individual staff credited for student inspiration and counseling more than circle": "Square praises specific staff by name and role: \"my history teacher inspired me\" and \"my son’s counselor, Lori Compton, is amazing,\" highlighting standout individual educators and counselors, whereas Circle offers positive statements about staff generally without naming individuals.",
  "circle describes explicit institutional support for arts, choir, and athletics more than square": "Circle states \"the choir is very well put together with an excellent teacher\" and \"The administration is very supportive of the arts and the music program and athletically, the school is doing well,\" giving program-level support for arts and sports not similarly described in Square (which mentions athletic areas but not arts programs).",
  "square reports problematic staff responses to bullying (victims punished, bullies unpunished) more than circle": "Square asserts a troubling disciplinary outcome: \"Supports bullying, punishes victims and leaves the bullies to continue bullying,\" a claim about staff responses that is more specific and accusatory than Circle's descriptions of fights and drama without assertions that victims are punished by staff."

  "circle reports a hostile student climate and ineffective discipline causing serious student harm more than square": "Circle contains multiple reports of sustained bullying, ostracism and weak enforcement—e.g. “I was cyber-bullied,” “some students had bullied and harassed another student for months on end and received no punishment,” and a reviewer claims they “literally suffer from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder” and would “dread walking into school.” Square contains no reports of bullying, safety lapses, or trauma and instead emphasizes positive community supports.",

  "circle reports contested and inequitable admissions practices more than square": "Circle includes detailed critique of magnet admissions disadvantaging BPS students—e.g. “Many middle class parents send their children to private school prior to applying... guess who gets in?”—whereas square provides no commentary on selective admissions or access issues.",
  "circle reports a narrow humanities focus and weak STEM offerings while square highlights broader opportunities and personalized exploration": "Circle explicitly warns “This is NOT the school for you if you are interested in Math, Technology and Science (STEM)” and notes required AP English Comp and AP World History with limited electives, while square says the district offers “opportunities not afforded to students in larger schools” and that students “don’t become just another number,” implying broader, personalized curricular exploration.",
  "circle documents inconsistent and controversial grading practices more than square": "Circle accuses the school of skewed grading policies—“CHS grades are unusually and intentionally skewed... an A starts at 95” and teachers were told to “limit the number of A's”—yet also contains another reviewer claiming students receive “grades ranging from 95-103” with minimal effort, indicating inconsistent grading experiences; square contains no grading-policy complaints.",

  "square reports small school size and personalized attention more than circle": "Square emphasizes scale and personalization—“It's small enough so they don't become just another number, yet there are so many opportunities for them to explore,” whereas circle repeatedly describes clique dynamics, ostracism, and a hostile social environment rather than individualized support."

  "circle demonstrates more responsive and supportive staff and health services than square": "Circle repeatedly names responsive staff and services—“The principal and office staff are excellent.   "square reports overcrowded classrooms and resource shortages more than circle": "Square states concrete capacity and resource problems: “The classrooms are overcrowded, the guidance counselors are not helpful, and resources are bare,” whereas Circle gives no indication of overcrowding or resource deficits and instead highlights strong program enjoyment.",
  "square reports systemic failures in administrative and counseling support more than circle": "Square contains multiple allegations of ineffective leadership and counseling: “Mr. Terrell, the Principle, is militant,” “The counselor, Patty Rollison, is disconnected,” and “Counselors don't care about the students,” while Circle describes welcoming staff and smooth administrative support for preschool transitions.",
  "square reports frequent student behavior, safety, and attendance problems more than circle": "Square repeatedly cites negative student conduct and safety/attendance issues: “there has been many fights recently,” “chaotic hallways,” “crime,” and “a large number of absences,” whereas Circle describes a “safe place of faith and respect” and does not mention fights, crime, or chronic absenteeism.",
  "square describes a specialized International Baccalaureate program that reviewers say is poorly implemented, whereas circle reports general academic strength without specialized programs": "Square repeatedly critiques IB implementation: “The 'idea' of the Thornton High School International Baccalaureate program drew us in, the execution is often times poor,” and “The IB program is an embarrassment,” while Circle praises general academic achievement (“Our kids are getting a great education”) and makes no mention of an IB or similar specialized program.",
  "square documents specific staff misconduct scandals more than circle": "Square reports concrete misconduct: “Their former band director had innapropriate relationships with students,” an explicit staff scandal absent from Circle, which contains no allegations of staff impropriety.",
  "square shows more teacher burnout and lack of individualized instruction than circle": "Square repeatedly notes teachers are overwhelmed and not meeting diverse learning needs: “The teachers are fantastic but are stressed out,” “Most teachers dont try to help students learn how they feel is best,” and “teachers... overwhelmed,” while Circle emphasizes individualized attention indirectly through welcoming transitions and high student self-worth without describing teacher stress." 
}"]

["{
  "circle reports stronger college-prep outcomes and advanced course opportunities than square": "Circle reviewers repeatedly cite measurable college-prep outcomes and coursework: “We have the highest SAT average in the area,” “Many people have gotten into great schools such as UNC, NC State, Clemson,” “AP classes are typically very well taught,” and mention dual enrollment at CPCC; square contains no comparable claims of strong AP/college-placement performance and instead says “With the exception of a few teachers, the academics are terrible.”",

  "square reports more gang and drug related safety concerns on campus than circle": "Square begins with an explicit safety claim: “There is a lot of drug and gang activity within the school and is not a safe environment,” and multiple reviewers question safety/cliques; circle mentions bullying, assaults, underage drinking/smoking and isolated safety incidents but does not include allegations of active gang/drug networks like square does (circle: “My child was bullied and assaulted on school campus,” and “Also a lot of underage drinking and smoking”).",

  "circle demonstrates stricter rules, heavier homework, and more rigid discipline enforcement than square": "Circle reviews repeatedly describe rigid enforcement and busywork: “They do enforce a dress code,” “The teachers push us to do our VERY best… homework is definitely extensive,” “very rigid administration… Little flexibility,” and students spending “more time in silent lunch and detention than learning useful material,” while square’s complaints focus on teacher quality and social dynamics rather than consistent school-wide heavy workload or systematic rule enforcement.",

  "circle requires organized parental involvement and operates as a lottery-based, small school-of-choice with a stronger small-school community feel than square": "Circle explicitly notes institutionalized family involvement and admission model: “This school is lottery based,” and “Serve 10 that allows each family serve 10 hrs of volunteering each year,” plus statements like “the school is small enough to feel your child is getting the attention they deserve”; square describes a larger district context with many community amenities and varied student groups but no formal family-service requirement or lottery admission.",

  "square shows more concrete administrative/operational errors and unhelpful clerical handling of student records than circle": "Square contains specific operational failures that impacted students: “the attendance staff for my school forgot to get me out of class for a dmv appointment… they also didn't excuse it which caused my grade to drop by 2 letters,” and reviewers say “Staff is useless and doesnt help solve ANY problems”; circle’s criticisms focus on policy inflexibility, tone, and responsiveness rather than clerical mistakes that directly altered grades/attendance.",

  "circle describes explicit curriculum and policy changes toward mandated social-justice training and identity programming more than square": "One circle reviewer details institutionalized curricular/policy shifts: “Teachers must undergo mandatory training in privilege and racial bias,” programs named “Mix It Up” and “Drop Everything and Talk,” and claims that “classic literature has been dropped from the curriculum,” whereas square contains no discussion of mandated social-justice curricula or staff trainings.",

  "circle contains recurring allegations of gender-biased treatment and distinctly negative experiences for male or female students more than square": "Circle includes multiple gender-specific complaints: “this school caters to young male students,” “administration ignores the needs of our intelligent young women,” and counterclaims that boys are punished more: “boys spend more time in silent lunch and detention,” while square’s complaints describe general cliques and student groups but do not allege systematic gender bias or differential treatment along sex lines.",

  "circle presents substantially more praise for teacher dedication and quality while square reports mostly indifferent or poor teacher engagement": "Many circle reviewers emphasize committed staff and effective teachers: “The teachers are great,” “LNC truly has a group of dedicated staff,” and “AP classes are typically very well taught,” whereas square reviewers repeatedly state the opposite generalization: “With the exception of a few teachers, the academics are terrible and most teachers could care less about their students' futures,” and “most of the teachers and staff members I've been squinted with were horrible.”",

  "square highlights proximity to municipal amenities and a more urban/main-street campus context more than circle": "Square mentions immediate community facilities and downtown adjacency as features: “There's a beautiful city library directly across the street, as well as City Hall,” “AHS is also next to Main Street and there are a lot of places to eat,” and “Police station is right next to the school,” while circle focuses on internal programs, campus academic offerings and a small charter model rather than nearby municipal facilities."
}"]

  "square shows inconsistent staff and guidance behavior (wide variability in support) more than circle": "Square contains directly conflicting reviewer accounts about staff responsiveness—one reviewer says “Guidance department would rather laugh in your face,” while another says “The guidance counselors are professional and caring,” demonstrating inconsistent practice; circle presents a single, consistent set of claims about teacher effectiveness and help opportunities (e.g. “Some of the teachers are not effective educators,” and “There are abundant opportunities for students to get help”).",
  "square reports both significant facility investment and concurrent maintenance problems more than circle": "Square names a ‘‘brand new school facility’’ and enthusiasm for high-tech programs—“Everyone is VERY excited the STEM and STEAM programs” and “Brand new school facility is a testament”—but also documents facility/maintenance shortfalls: “Apparently the air conditioner is broken,” indicating simultaneous investment and unresolved maintenance; circle makes no facility or infrastructure claims.",
  "square reports overcrowding and disruptive scheduling problems more than circle": "Square directly reports capacity and schedule issues: “The school has too many students for the number of teachers,” “teachers are more concerned with switching rooms 10 times a day,” and “There are a ridiculous number of ‘half days’,” whereas circle makes no mention of crowding or scheduling problems.",

  "circle reports abundant academic help availability more than square": "Circle explicitly states ‘‘There are abundant opportunities for students to get help with their studies,’’ a clear, succinct claim about on-site academic support; square includes mixed reports about teacher availability (some say teachers go above and beyond, others say teachers don’t stay after class), so circle provides the more straightforward claim of abundant help.",

  "circle shows explicit, institutionalized faith and daily religion practice while square does not": "Circle repeatedly describes a faith-centered environment: 'Religion and prayer are a daily part of a students life a DeSales' and 'Faith, Family, Tradition,' whereas Square contains no description of daily religious practice or an explicitly faith-based mission.",
  "square reports more teacher and staff inaction on harassment and discipline than circle": "Square contains direct testimony that 'I have been harassed and the teachers while fully aware of it yet most of them did nothing but stand by and let it happen,' and describes inconsistent discipline, while Circle includes multiple statements that 'trouble is never tolerated' and that 'The Administration works very diligently to keep on top of the problems.'",
  "circle describes broader, numerically large extracurricular and service opportunities than square": "Circle lists concrete breadth: 'over 30 clubs to choose from, 25 Varsity sports, a fantastic arts program and multiple service opportunities,' while Square mentions clubs and events (math team, theme days) but gives no comparable counts or breadth.",
  "square reports more severe school security incidents (bomb threat and lockdown) than circle": "Square states 'there has been a bomb threat and a soft lockdown,' identifying specific serious security events; Circle includes behavioral and discipline complaints but does not report bomb threats or lockdowns.",
  "square reports problematic school law-enforcement behavior inside the building while circle does not": "Square criticizes an 'untrustworthy cop' who 'gives the evil eye' and selectively enforces rules at lunch, whereas Circle contains no mention of on-campus police or problematic officer behavior.",
  "square reports more poor teacher–parent communication and inconsistent class information than circle": "Square offers a parent's account: 'Communication with the teachers was poor and inconsistent... Only a small percentage bother to update their class websites in a timely fashion,' but Circle reviews emphasize supportive teachers and administration with no parallel pattern of poor parent communication.",
  "square reports punitive treatment and poor support for students with behavioral or special needs leading to expulsions while circle does not": "Square asserts that students with ADHD/ODD are 'accepted... only to kick them out' and that 'manifestation meeting are really expulsion meetings,' while Circle contains no reports of systematic expulsions of special-needs students.",
  "circle contains more criticism and discussion of specific administrative financial/structural decisions (debt, curriculum 'double math') than square": "Circle includes concrete administrative critiques—'the administration has this place so in debt' and debate over the 'double math' policy—whereas Square's administrative complaints focus on staff attitudes and discipline, not school debt or a named curriculum policy controversy.",
  "square shows more concrete anecdotal evidence that rigorous STEM coursework translated into college readiness than circle, which emphasizes matriculation rates with mixed preparedness claims": "Square gives a specific outcome: 'I received a C in Calc BC and now I am getting solid As in my math class at UIUC,' indicating college-level readiness from rigorous courses; Circle cites '98% go on to college' but also contains reviewer claims that 'grade inflation' leaves students unprepared."
}"]

  "circle reports inability or refusal to accommodate special education needs (staffing or paperwork) more than square": "Circle states administrators told the parent “they could not help my son and that they did not have the staff” and that because the IEP paperwork wasn’t filled out “they said that they could not help my son,” showing both staffing shortages and procedural refusal; square mentions no lack of special education capacity or procedural exclusion.",

  "square offers substantial college credit/dual enrollment opportunities more than circle": "Square notes “there are enough college credits you can receive to nearly complete your freshman year of college,” indicating structured dual‑credit/college prep opportunities absent from circle’s account.",

["{
  "circle reports stronger academic outcomes and institutional recognition (college preparation, scholarships, ratings) than square": "Circle reviewers cite explicit college-preparatory success and measurable recognition: e.g., “prepares her for college (in the 7th and 8th grade)”, “GREAT SCHOLARSHIPS ... more than $4 million in scholarships”, and “rated 1+ by CPS this year.” Square contains no comparable claims of scholarships, college prep outcomes, or high official ratings.",
  "square reports more severe safety incidents and chronic student misconduct (stabbings, fires, fights, second‑hand smoke) than circle": "Square recounts explicit violent and hazardous incidents: “a student was stabbed in the hallway,” “one kid set a fire in the class,” repeated fights and complaints about being “the victim of second hand smoke.” Circle complains about disrespect and painful social-emotional transitions but does not describe comparable violent or arson incidents.",
  "square reports pervasive social promotion and students advanced without mastery more than circle": "Square details systematic promotion despite failure—“promoting students to the next grade up even if they got F's... pushed into Algebra 2... only about 50% of the 12th grade class has enough credits to graduate”—a theme absent from Circle, which emphasizes rigorous, college‑level coursework and teacher expectations.",
  "circle highlights stronger extracurricular and performing arts programs and higher student participation than square": "Circle explicitly praises performing arts and high club/athletics engagement: “The academic and performing arts programs are top‑drawer. Clubs and athletics are heavily subscribed.” Square mentions some promising small learning communities and academies, but lacks the sustained praise for broad, well‑subscribed arts and extracurricular programming found in Circle.",
  "square describes worse physical facilities and prison‑like building conditions than circle": "Square repeatedly calls the building dilapidated and prison‑like—“The school is old and not maintained,” “the inside of the school looks like a prison”—whereas Circle mentions overcrowding and a planned move to a separate building but does not describe pervasive facility decay.",
  "square reports higher teacher turnover and chronic substitute coverage than circle": "Square says “an astounding number of classes are STILL being covered by subs, or NO ONE, a full semester into the year” and notes teachers are leaving; Circle, by contrast, contains multiple endorsements of “phenomenal” and “skilled” teachers and “caring counselors,” with no claims of widespread unfilled classes.",
  "circle reports overcrowding and harmful mixed‑age integration affecting middle schoolers more than square": "Circle repeatedly flags overcrowding and problematic 7th/8th grader interaction with older students—“severely overcrowded,” “7th & 8th graders would have little to no interaction with high school students... flat out lie,” and “social emotional transition has been quite painful”—a specific mixed‑age transition problem not described in Square.",
  "square attributes school failings more to district‑level bureaucracy and lack of resources than circle does": "Square explicitly blames higher‑level administration and resource constraints: “teachers and admin are still under the thumb of a blind district office; and hands are tied by bureaucracy, lack of funding, inadequate resources,” whereas Circle’s criticisms focus more on local overcrowding, specific administrators (e.g., “principal is unreachable”), and staff attitudes rather than sustained blame of a district bureaucracy."
}"]

["{
  "circle has more extensive specialized performance and athletic facilities than square": "Circle explicitly lists multiple specialized spaces—\"three theatre spaces, two gyms, a professional dance studio and a pool\"—while Square only praises programs (band, journalism) and mentions \"advanced facilities\" once without detailing multiple specialized spaces.",
  "square highlights an outstanding journalism program more than circle": "Square repeatedly praises its journalism department and student newspapers—\"outstanding journalism department...monthly newsletters are, in fact, not the newspapers...be proud of the children who put together such a paper\"—whereas Circle emphasizes theatre/performing arts and does not single out a journalism program.",
  "square reports administrative disengagement and punitive emphasis more than circle": "Multiple Square reviewers accuse administration of poor outreach and misplaced priorities—\"administration cares more about the dress code...they very seldom reach out to the students...the principle has a moto of Student's First but that is not the way\"—while Circle describes \"the most caring team of teachers and counselors\" and an interim principal praised as a positive change.",
  "square reports concrete safety and cleanliness problems (bullying, drug use, filthy hallways) whereas circle reports inclusivity and support instead": "Square contains direct safety/cleanliness complaints: \"the school hallways remain filthy...I don't feel safe from bullying, discrimination, and, more importantly, drug use...walk behind a student smoking in the hallways.\" Circle, conversely, says students are \"talented, smart, friendly\" and notes \"Very good support for ADHD, very inclusive to everyone.\"",
  "circle presents more consistent statements of academic rigor and steady improvement than square's mixed academic outcomes": "Circle asserts \"classes are rigorous...steady improvement in test scores\" and calls itself \"an award-winning school\" while Square contains conflicting outcome claims—some say \"so many students are graduating...and they are not prepared for college,\" while others list Ivy League acceptances and National Merit awards—showing inconsistent academic outcome reports.",
  "square emphasizes strict dress code enforcement more than circle": "Square reviewers repeatedly claim the school and staff \"care more about the dress code\" and that dress code is \"strict and adhered to,\" whereas Circle includes no mention of dress code enforcement.",
  "square reports teacher role overload and availability problems more than circle": "Square includes reviewer observations that \"some of the teachers have multiple jobs, like also being a coach and they're not very helpful if you're having trouble,\" suggesting role overload reduces instructional support; Circle describes teachers as \"absolutely wonderful\" and \"the most caring team,\" with no mention of split roles harming availability.",
  "circle describes broader, centralized performing-arts and elective breadth for diverse student interests more than square": "Circle claims it \"offers every program you could wish for\" and has a \"well-rounded curriculum and seemingly endless electives,\" focusing on performing arts and multiple programs; Square mentions a \"wide array of electives\" and strong band/journalism but concentrates praise on specific departments rather than claiming across-the-board program breadth.",
  "square reports clique-driven unwelcoming student social dynamics more than circle": "Square reviewers state \"there are a lot of cliques there and the students are not all like and welcoming...Most of the friends I have here came from a different district like me and didn't know anybody,\" while Circle characterizes students as \"friendly, and down-to-earth\" and inclusive."
}"]

["{
  "circle shows more advanced coursework and recent academic improvement whereas square reports absence of gifted programs and persistent weak fundamentals": "Circle reports growth in higher-level math and recent improvement—\"this year's Senior Class...we now have two Calculus periods\" and \"there are so many students signed up\"—while Square explicitly states a long-standing absence of advanced programming: \"There were no good programs like GT in Newton\" and criticizes continuing weak instruction: \"I got 8 more years of Kindergarten with sporadic good advice.\"",
  "circle describes active staff-led culture and character initiatives whereas square does not": "Circle documents a school-run kindness effort and supportive staff: \"Goodness campaign...The staff is rewarding acts of kindness\" and \"The staff and the students are amazing...like a second family,\" whereas Square gives no examples of current staff-led culture programs or supportive initiatives inside the school.",
  "circle reports athletic favoritism and grade inflation for athletes whereas square does not": "Circle alleges grade inflation tied to athletics: \"Teachers will give students good grades if they are in the football team...The student was below average in English but still received an 'A'.\" Square contains no similar claim about athletic favoritism affecting grades.",
  "circle reports disciplinary segregation and on-campus safety/group-color concerns (alternative school proximity and dress color warning) whereas square does not": "Circle warns of a nearby alternative school for troubled students—\"The alternative school for bad kids is less than two hundred yards away!!!\"—and a peer-safety/dress-color caution: \"Just remember to not dress in all BLUE!\" Square does not mention an alternative placement program, nearby disciplinary facility, or dress-color safety warnings.",
  "square attributes individual student success to prior schools and family background while circle attributes success to current school supports and programs": "Square emphasizes external and preexisting advantages as the reason for later success: \"I was lucky...coming from a family of educators\" and credits earlier elementary GT for career success, \"with the strong fundamentals I got at NHS I have had a very successful career,\" whereas Circle credits school-based supports and programs for student progress: \"if your child is a dedicated student, they will go far after attending LOHS\" and cites in-school changes like new teachers and expanding Calculus enrollment."
}"]

["{
  "circle exhibits more consistent and responsive school leadership and administration than square": "Circle: reviewers state “Strong school system administration and great high school leadership” and praise how the “Principal rallied staff, parents and community leaders to get us back to virtual, then hybrid, then in person.” Square: reviewers complain “There are a lot of areas that the admin need to work on” and describe staff churn (“many staff have changed over the years”), indicating weaker, less consistent leadership.",
  "square shows more frequent safety incidents and requires visible security presence than circle": "Square explicitly notes safety problems and visible security: “For safety reasons they have a police officer on duty and multiple security guards” and “there has been a lot of fights at Logan” including references to “gang fights and security problems.” Circle contains no reports of fights or required security presence.",
  "square suffers more severe overcrowding and teacher capacity strain than circle": "Square reviewers repeatedly report size and crowding problems: “The sheer size of the student body… school is way too overcrowded,” and “the school has way to many students for the teachers to keep up with.” Circle instead highlights facility improvement and does not report overcrowding.",
  "circle offers more consistent advanced academic course options and college preparation than square": "Circle notes a broad, reliable curriculum: “Compare its academic programs… you'll see that DHS has a greater choice in AP, Honors and CP level courses” and that students were “very well prepared for college.” Square mentions programs like ICL and ROP and some elite admits but also contains multiple complaints that curriculum is “subpar” or not preparing students for college.",
  "square shows more inconsistent instructional quality and reliance on low-effort assignments than circle": "Square reviewers allege poor instruction and low-rigor practices: “teachers don't teach anything,” and “Many teachers rely on group projects where students rely on internet searches to write up one slide a piece and loose out on learning.” Circle reviewers describe hands-on care and academic help: “a teacher or administrator cared for my teen… Assistance is always available.”",
  "square presents greater variability in student outcomes, producing both elite college admits and students unprepared for college, compared with circle": "Square contains both high-end success stories (“a few from my graduating class who now attend Harvard, Brown, and Stanford”) and warnings that students were unprepared (“her college career was at risk if she stayed at this school,” “you could not get a chance at UC CSU Or private college admissions after graduation from JLHS”), whereas circle reports uniformly that students were “very well prepared for college” and had “plenty of good college choices.”",
  "circle demonstrates stronger continuous individual student support (counseling and guidance) than square": "Circle gives concrete continuity examples: “he had the same counselor from day one” and families report sustained support “From the first information request call to graduation, a teacher or administrator cared for my teen… for 4 full years.” Square gives no examples of consistent counseling and instead cites rude office staff and churn.",
  "circle shows more active facility investment and modernization than square": "Circle explicitly reports capital investment: “They are building a new facility now 2011 and it's plans are amazing.” Square mentions a “beautiful campus” but provides no evidence of current construction or modernization projects.",
  "square emphasizes vocational programs and college-scouted athletics more than circle": "Square highlights career and athletic pipelines: “ROP classes that give you experience to prepare you… if you have a child looking for a scholarship for a sport in college James Logan is one of the few schools that get's scouts from Universities.” Circle notes athletics abundance but does not mention ROP pathways or university scouting.",
  "square raises racial equity and community trust concerns that circle does not": "Square includes explicit concerns about race and district trust: “There are a lot of areas that the admin need to work on. Mostly importantly their relationship with the African American race” and warnings that “the entire NHUSD school district can't be trusted.” Circle, by contrast, emphasizes a welcoming reception for newcomers and inclusive culture without such equity complaints."
}"]

  "square reports multiple specialized magnet programs and students leaving home schools whereas circle does not": "Square names several magnet programs and the magnet-driven enrollment pattern: “NESA/ISA/STEM … many of the kids leave their home zoned campuses to attend the great magnet programs offered at LEE (NESA/ISA/STEM),” whereas Circle makes no mention of magnet programs or students transferring in for specialty tracks.",
  "circle reports reduced elective offerings and heavy focus on standardized testing while square does not describe that": "Circle states a curricular narrowing and test emphasis: “there are only basic classes now and not enough elective courses… Too much attention is focused on standardized tests,” a complaint absent from Square, which instead highlights program variety and arts (NESA) offerings.",
  "square reports small class sizes and more individualized attention compared with circle": "Square explicitly notes smaller classes and attendant benefits: “class sizes are small” and “the teachers are excellent and caring,” whereas Circle does not report small class sizes or individualized attention (it emphasizes general past quality and current disappointments about offerings).",
  "circle describes poor responsiveness for basic administrative and technical help while square describes proactive administrative communication": "Circle lists concrete failures in simple administrative/tech support: “locker combination problems, login problems for parent resources, or makeup homework… nearly impossible to get assistance with,” whereas Square praises administrative communication: “The Principal seems to run an outstanding school and is also very communicative… The principal stays in contact with the parents via weekly emails.”",
  "square documents explicit staff hostility incidents (yelling and hostile librarians) that circle does not": "Square recounts direct hostile staff behavior during enrollment and library interactions: “The older lady in the counselor's office was yelling at students non stop… 'what do you 2ant ehat do you need speak up!!!'” and “the librarians are needlessly hostile,” while Circle’s complaints concern rule unevenness and service problems, not staff yelling or overt hostility.",
  "square describes a positive peer climate and supportive environment while circle reports unequal rule enforcement and parental disappointment": "Square emphasizes student conduct and supportive atmosphere: “The Lee students … have been uniformly respectful and kind” and “We have been very happy with the positive way the kids treat each other… I love the supportive environment,” whereas Circle reports differential rule application and overall disappointment: “Rules apply differently to certain students… I feel like my kids deserve a better education and it's very disappointing overall.”"
}"]

["{
  "square reports severe overcrowding and high student to teacher ratio more than circle": "Square repeatedly describes overcrowding and staffing strain with phrases like \"how crowded it was the student to teacher ratio\", \"the school is overpopulated\", and \"too many students for the teachers to help\", whereas Circle gives no indication of overcrowding and describes a typical small-town high school instead.",

  "square reports drug availability among students while circle does not": "Square explicitly reports West is \"notorious for drug availability among students\", a safety/behavior issue absent from Circle's description.",
  "square exhibits lax discipline and a student run culture (permissive device use, roaming, disrespect to staff) more than circle": "Square claims \"Students are allowed to text message in class and listen to their ipods\", students are \"seen in the halls during class\", and \"the students run the school\" with \"level of disrespect from kids to the teachers is absolutely horrid\"; Circle makes no similar claims about permissive behavior or students running the school.",
  "square reports administrative and disciplinary favoritism and unreliable evidence handling more than circle": "Square describes punishments \"influenced by favoritism\" and a case where a student was suspended but administration later said \"there was no video\", indicating problematic discipline administration; Circle criticizes teachers for writing off students but includes no reports of favoritism or unreliable investigatory procedures by administrators.",
  "circle reports pronounced socioeconomic stratification leading teachers to focus on college bound students and neglect lower income students more than square": "Circle quantifies a lower-income group (\"about 12-15 percent\") and states \"many teachers write off students they do not think are college material and only focus their efforts on kids who are going to college\", describing a socioeconomic gap driving instructional attention that Square does not similarly quantify or frame.",
  "square reports worse postsecondary outcomes and explicit low college matriculation rates more than circle": "Square gives a concrete outcome statistic: \"Only %46 of graduates make it to a 4-year university from West High School\", and reviewers link school practices to students who \"can't make it at college\", whereas Circle implies most students are college-bound and offers no comparable low matriculation statistic.",
  "square reports athletic staff prioritizing sports at the expense of instruction more than circle": "Square accuses athletic staff of \"football coaches who don't teach but only hand-out packets\" and says the school is \"focusing too much on the football program\", while Circle notes that \"Football is VERY big\" but does not allege coaches neglect instruction.",
  "square notes absence of specific programs or desired facilities (no JROTC, no pool) while circle does not": "Square contains a reviewer upset that the school is \"NOT having a JROTC program\" and requests \"maybe put a pool inside\", indicating gaps in specific programming/facilities; Circle mentions sports offerings but does not report missing programmatic options or requested facilities.",
  "circle presents the school as an above average, small town community oriented high school more than square": "Circle summarizes the experience as \"overall an above average school for East Texas\" and describes a \"typical blue collar middle class small town high school\" with \"faculty overall is above average\", whereas Square contains numerous complaints about overcrowding, safety, discipline, and poor outcomes despite some positive reviews."

  "circle shows much poorer staff responsiveness and parent communication than square": "Circle cites multiple communication and responsiveness failures: “they don’t know when a student is even present or absent! … No one knows what’s going on and no one answers the phone there!” and students’ pleas were ignored (“ive made many attemps to get help but theyre all ignored by staff”), while Square gives concrete evidence of staff responsiveness and counseling support (“Mr. Nicholson was there for me… The councerl are great… staff is very supportive”).",

  "circle enforces stricter discipline, uniform and phone policies than square": "Circle includes explicit descriptions of tight enforcement: complaints about rules such as “you can not wear a 'colored' undershirt,” phone confiscation policies (“if your phone is in your pocket...they are taking it”), and students saying the school felt “really strict,” while Square contains complaints about administrative laxity around behavior rather than descriptions of strict uniform/phone enforcement.",

  "circle reports greater parent and community involvement and visible staff commitment than square": "Circle explicitly says “Building tremendous parent and community involvement” and repeatedly highlights staff commitment—“I was very impressed with the level of commitment by the educational staff”—whereas Square contains more commentary about parental divisions and reputational disputes and fewer statements emphasizing broad parent/community engagement.",
  "square reports worse facility condition and need for building upgrades than circle": "Square reviewers repeatedly note the physical plant needs work—“the facility needs to be updated... the building needs a facelift,” “over 50 years old and needs to be badly remodeled”—while Circle’s comments focus on programs, staff, and rules and do not raise facility-condition concerns.",
  "circle describes more formalized student leadership and structured extracurricular pathways than square": "Circle lists organized leadership opportunities (ambassadors, student government) and multiple clubs/sports with students describing roles like “I am cheer captain,” and leadership-building goals, while Square mentions sports and cheer but gives fewer concrete examples of structured leadership programs or pathways to leadership throughout the reviews."

  "circle emphasizes college acceptance and longer term student success outcomes more than square": "Circle directly credits the school with outcomes: \"This school was integral in my college acceptance and subsequent success,\" while Square focuses on programs and supports and only implicitly links those to future outcomes.",
