["{
  "circle has a pronounced specialized STEM Scholars/honors program with strong teacher engagement more than square": "Multiple reviewers repeatedly praise a concentrated Scholars/engineering focus at the school: “The Scholars program is a great place for my son, he loves science, math & engineering,” and “He is challenged WITHOUT being OVERWHELMED… engineering classes both years… engineering teacher is super smart.” Square mentions AP/CCP and advanced classes but does not center a single, repeatedly referenced specialized scholars STEM program.",
  "square displays more explicit measurable academic outcomes and college-credit pathways than circle": "Square reviewers cite concrete outcomes and pathways: “this year our OGT results are ranked in the top 50 in the state,” and “older kids were accepted at OSU and had at least a year of credits from CCP and AP classes.” Circle contains many qualitative college-prep comments (e.g. “will be well, prepared for college”) but lacks the same numeric metrics and college-credit evidence.",
  "circle shows selective attention favoring honors/scholars students while neglecting regular students more than square": "Several circle reviewers claim differential treatment: “the teachers seem to only care for the honors students and have drifted away from the regular students,” and parents complain regular classes “barely ever explain it correctly.” Square raises barriers to honors placement (waivers) but does not contain the same theme of day-to-day teacher favoritism toward honors students.",
  "square reports more allegations of racial staff underrepresentation and hallway racial name-calling incidents than circle": "Square contains multiple accusations about race and staffing: “If you are an African American, you are overlooked,” and “racial comments are rampant in the hallways, and the teachers pretends they don't hear it.” Circle, by contrast, repeatedly highlights diversity positively (e.g. “There is a diverse population of both student and teachers”) and includes no comparable reports of racial name-calling.",
  "circle reports more acute teacher and counselor unresponsiveness to struggling or absent students than square": "Circle reviewers describe specific failures to support absent or struggling students: “If you ask for help they don't attempt to accommodate you… The counselor barely ever returns calls and its nearly impossible to make an appointment,” and teachers “will often not give you work from the previous day nor even help you to acquire notes.” Square includes some complaints about minimal parent communication but not the same cluster of counselor nonresponse and missed-work refusals.",
  "square exhibits greater parental and community involvement and public defender voices than circle": "Square reviewers emphasize active parent engagement and parent-authored defenses: “A lot of parents were super-involved… Many of us are there all during the summer and get together to share and plan,” and multiple comments come explicitly from ‘a parent and teacher’ defending the school. Circle notes engaged scholars parents, but square foregrounds broader community/parent advocacy repeatedly.",
  "square shows administrative organizational weakness and accountability issues more than circle": "Square contains explicit administrative critique: “Most of the administrators were average at best… They could be unorganized, and lack accountability on certain social issues.” Circle, in contrast, includes repeated praise of leadership: “Mr. Alonso the principal is a dynamic man with a clear vision” and “The administration works well together.”",
  "circle reports an on-site assigned police presence inside the school more than square": "Circle explicitly notes formal law-enforcement assignment: “The Chicago Police Officers assigned to the school are top notch and assist in so many ways.” Square only references school security guards enforcing rules and does not report an assigned police presence.",
  "square offers a broader variety of extracurricular activities than circle": "Square highlights a wide extracurricular menu: “a variety of extracurricular activities… almost every academic opportunity you could want from clubs, to advanced math, AP, and honors classes.” Circle contains the opposite complaint from multiple reviewers: “there aren't enough extracurricular activities.”",
  "circle reports student drug-selling incidents inside the school whereas square does not": "One circle reviewer warns of student drug activity: “the people here are druggies, constantly trying to sell to my child as i was told by him.” No reviewer in the square set describes student drug-selling or similar substance-related incidents.",
  "circle emphasizes individualized special-education support and professional handling of meltdowns more than square": "Circle provides a detailed example of special-education practice: “Our son is in the sped program… From day one, he was treated well… When our son has a meltdown it is handled professionally and effectively in a very safe manner.” Square praises its special-ed program in general terms (“very good special Ed program”) but lacks the same concrete descriptive episode of individualized crisis handling."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports a severe off-campus assault causing concussion and small brain bleed more than square": "Circle explicitly describes a violent robbery/assault off campus that “gave him a concussion and small brain bleed,” whereas Square lists bullying and attacks but does not report a single described incident causing a documented concussion/brain bleed.",

  "circle describes administration and counselors actively devaluing academic recovery more than square": "Circle recounts counselors telling a parent “not to worry, he didn't need those anyway” and offering Teacher's Aid placements instead of course retakes, and calls the administration “truly terrible administration and counselors,” showing counselor-driven academic disengagement not present in Square.",
  "circle reports athletic coaches enforcing policies that block academic opportunities with unresponsive athletic administration more than square": "Circle details a varsity girls coach who denied a student early release for a prep course, the athletic director saying “thats his policy,” and the vice principal refusing to intervene—“Whey have a Vice principal in athletics if coaches can do what they want.” Square includes no comparable example of athletics blocking academics.",
  "circle highlights strong AP offerings and teacher effort more than square": "Circle explicitly praises that “The A.P program is outstanding” and that “faculty at this school is terrific everyone cares about student achievement,” while Square complains about weak college/SAT preparedness and poor senior curriculum without noting advanced AP program strength.",
  "square reports implementation of a formal PBIS program and measurable behavioral improvement more than circle": "Square states Somersworth High “implemented the Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports (PBIS) a couple years back and it has done amazing things for the kids, school, test scores and overall morale,” a specific programmatic intervention not mentioned in Circle.",
  "square reports the presence of vocational/real-life education programs more than circle": "Square notes the school “helps teens learn real-life education with its vocational center combined with regular high school classes,” while Circle includes no description of vocational or CTE offerings.",

  "square documents inconsistent or poor instructional practice and opaque grading from teachers more than circle": "Square gives concrete classroom/assessment failures—an A- turned to an F after a single final, a research paper graded 45 with no explanation, teachers giving only one worksheet for an 84-minute period—depicting instructional inconsistency that Circle does not emphasize (Circle praises hardworking teachers despite other issues).",

  "square depicts a mixed social climate—strong school spirit and academy 'families' alongside cliques and self‑centered students—whereas circle portrays pervasive drama and heartache": "Square contains both positive social markers (\"Anyone who says that the school lacks spirit has obviously never been to a pep rally...\", \"each academy is like it's own little family\") and warnings about cliques and \"fake\" students, while circle offers only social negativity (\"it's all drama and heartache\").",

  "square provides more specialized academic programs, routine tutoring, and college partnerships than circle": "Square reviewers list concrete supports and programs: “Technology Magnet,” “CPDA magnet,” “tutoring daily before and after school,” and proximity to “Valley College is right next door.” Circle’s review mentions no magnet programs, structured tutoring, or college partnerships.",

  "square shows greater variability in teacher quality and classroom experience while circle mainly reports unprofessional or lax teachers": "Square contains polarized teacher reports — positive: “Teachers are seasoned… Teachers are dedicated,” and negative: “All the teachers, except for a couple magnet teachers, hate their lives… The math teachers there are a joke.” Circle consistently reports poor teacher conduct: “some of the teachers seem very lacksidaisical and unprofessional.”",
  "square experiences overcrowded classes more than circle": "Square explicitly states “Classes are of course overcrowded and inadequately taught for the most part,” and references large-school scale (e.g. many clubs, 6A). Circle’s entry makes no note of overcrowding or large class sizes.",
  "circle reports lower graduation outcomes while square reports improving metrics and college placements": "Circle: reviewer attributes poor success directly — “I understand ‘why’ their graduation rate is so low.” Square: reviewers cite improving academic indicators and outcomes — “Grant's API scores are up… they hit their API growth goals,” and “I have had 2 kids go to top universities after graduating from Grant.”",
  "square includes reviewer concerns about resource allocation and athletics prioritization that circle does not": "Square: one reviewer alleges misallocation—“I feel money is being taken away from the student programs and given to the football team… I feel it should [be] audited.” Circle’s review contains no mention of budget priorities or athletic funding concerns."
}"]

  "square reports acute safety, bullying, and administrative safety-decision problems more than circle": "Square contains explicit safety and climate complaints: “I’ve seen multiple cases of bullying and harrasment… Most if not all of our neighboring had a snow day because the roads are dangerous but not Westborough… they are valuing the education more than the safety of the students,” while circle has no comparable pattern of general bullying or school-level safety policy criticisms.",

["{
  "circle shows more administrative and guidance failures causing real student harm than square": "Circle describes concrete guidance/administration breakdowns: “We transferred from out of state and have had nothing but problems with transfer of credits,” “My child was scheduled wrong by the counselor, which led him to not graduate on time,” and “The guidance counselors have got to be the worst I've ever seen,” whereas Square states administrators and teachers “work with student to achieve” with no comparable reports of scheduling, transcript, or graduation errors.",
  "circle reports bullying, racial discrimination, and inadequate staff response while square does not": "Circle contains multiple incidents of hostile social climate and poor response: “If you're non-white, you will see a lot of discrimination…My son experienced it on a daily basis by students, and sadly by teachers as well,” and “The teachers witness bullying and yet do nothing,” whereas Square makes no mention of bullying or discrimination and instead describes a caring community.",
  "circle documents inconsistent teacher professionalism and favoritism more than square": "Circle gives examples of unprofessional teacher behavior and favoritism: “some will openly talk rudely about a student behind their back,” “a select few teachers that really care,” and “a lot of favoritism,” while Square portrays teachers as uniformly positive: “teachers seem very nice and want to teach the kids” and “Teachers and administrators work with student to achieve.”",
  "circle details broader named specialized programs and extracurricular breadth than square": "Circle lists numerous structured programs and activities by name—“Honors class, AP (Advance Placement) classes, and have an Engineering Academy as well as a Health Sciences Academy,” plus dual enrollment and many sports and fine arts—whereas Square only briefly notes AP offerings and general extracurricular availability: “AP offerings good even with a small rural high school.”",
  "circle reports limited in-person course availability and reliance on online courses while square does not": "Despite naming many programs, Circle also admits constrained in-person options and reliance on the state virtual school: “The limited class selection is sure to put off any transfer students, although the online class system provided by NCVPS helps to alleviate some of the limited class choices,” a dynamic not mentioned in Square.",
  "circle reports outdated, cramped campus facilities more than square": "Circle states negative facility conditions: “The school is old, outdated and way too small,” and “The campus itself is pretty small in size,” while Square praises small classroom size as an instructional advantage without reporting poor building condition: “the small classroom size i think allows for a better education.”",
  "circle emphasizes athletics dominating school culture more than square": "Circle explicitly claims academics are secondary to sports: “The school revolves around sports,” and multiple reviewers complain athletics overshadow preparation, whereas Square makes no claim that sports dominate and focuses on academics and standards.",
  "square highlights small class size as an educational benefit more than circle": "Square foregrounds class size as a pedagogical strength—“the small classroom size i think allows for a better education for the kids..” —while Circle mentions small campus size only in mixed or negative contexts (crowding/outdated) and does not present small class size as a clear instructional advantage."
}"]

  "circle highlights outstanding fine arts and athletic programs more than square": "Circle names \"Outstanding... fine arts and athletic programs\" directly; Square only notes that kids \"appreciate the sports, music, theater, and clubs that are offered\" without describing them as outstanding.",
  "circle describes an explicit faith‑based mission culture that square does not": "Circle asserts \"Franciscan philosophy evident in attitude of students, parents, alumni, faculty and staff,\" whereas Square contains no mention of a schoolwide religious or mission philosophy.",
  "circle emphasizes a large suburban campus footprint while square emphasizes smaller school size and broad participation": "Circle specifies a \"70 acre suburban campus,\" implying large grounds, while Square praises an \"ideal\" smaller size that offers \"ample activity opportunities, yet small enough to allow participation and leadership from even the quietest of kids.\"",
  "square reports defensive staff and lack of accountability more than circle": "Square includes \"I've noticed a lot of defensiveness from staff and administration\" and \"There is no accountability,\" complaints not present in Circle's descriptions of programs and campus.",
  "square reports delayed student support and a reactive \"disaster recovery\" approach that circle does not": "Square quotes a counselor: \"Students who fall through the cracks aren't given any real help until 11th grade... they go into disaster recovery mode and just try to get the student graduated,\" a specific operational critique absent from Circle.",
  "square reports staff misconduct and bullying by staff while circle does not": "Square contains a direct allegation: \"my kids were mentally abused and bulled by staff,\" whereas Circle offers no reports of staff abuse or mistreatment.",
  "square reports student outflow to other districts more than circle": "Square states \"NR students are increasingly going to Hudson and other districts, not vice versa,\" indicating net attrition or competition with neighboring districts; Circle makes no such claim.",
  "circle frames excellence as part of everyday culture whereas square frames mixed performance and inconsistency in outcomes": "Circle claims \"Excellence without pretentiousness\" and lists program strengths as part of its culture; Square mixes praise (e.g. some kids \"love their teachers\" and opportunities exist) with concrete complaints about support, accountability, and outcomes, portraying an inconsistent performance pattern."
}"]

["{
  "square offers more extensive AP/advanced college‑credit coursework and more highly credentialed teachers than circle": "Square repeatedly highlights college-preparatory breadth and instructor credentials: reviewers note “many faculty members who had their doctorates,” “AP classes,” “offered advanced classes for college credit, more in fact than any other in the city,” and students who could CLEP college courses; circle describes some rigor but contains specific complaints about math focus and mobility into advanced tracks (“if your child is not placed in advanced classes freshman year, it is extremely difficult to move up into them”).",
  "square reports stronger concrete alumni college outcomes and scholarship success than circle": "Square reviewers give concrete outcome claims: “Both of my sons graduated from Grissom with full scholarships,” alumni recount college/graduate‑school success and long professional careers; circle contains softer statements that students felt “well prepared for college” but lacks the repeated concrete scholarship/alumni‑success claims found in square.",
  "square provides less individualized support for struggling or less‑motivated students than circle": "Square reviewers explicitly warn it is a “sink or swim environment,” saying “Parents won't get much meaningful help when they are trying to bring along a well‑behaved, but struggling student” and that teachers are “stretched too thin to be of significant help to all of their students.” By contrast circle includes multiple reports of flexible, coaching‑style support: “teachers have been very flexible and worked with us to fit our needs,” and “Rigorous academics balanced by support and coaching where needed.”",
  "circle emphasizes a deliberately nurturing, community‑oriented environment and pastoral support more than square": "Multiple circle reviews praise an inclusive, supportive culture and whole‑student development: “outstanding education in an extremely supportive environment,” “the entire young woman is fostered at SMA,” “learning experiences beyond the classroom, such as volunteering, school retreats,” and many student/parent testimonials about feeling supported and encouraged—claims that are far more prominent in circle than in square.",
  "circle is explicitly a faith‑based, single‑sex (girls) institution with faith formation activities while square is a secular coeducational public school": "Circle reviews discuss Archdiocese affiliation, faith formation and retreats and explicitly frame education for girls (“giving all the girls an equal chance,” “shaping the next generation of women”), e.g. “SMA gives us a window to see the Catholic faith” and “school retreats”; square reviews describe public‑school programs (Army JROTC, large AP offerings) and do not reference religious formation, indicating a secular coed environment.",
  "circle reports active expansion and enrollment growth with concerns about rising class sizes more than square": "Circle reviewers warn of recent enrollment increases and growing pains: “last year the school increased enrollment from about 25 to 50 students,” parents should “ask some hard questions… what the school is doing to insure that class sizes do not increase,” and multiple notes of classes at ~25–30 students; these expansion and enrollment‑growth concerns are a recurring theme in circle but not in square.",
  "square reports overcrowding and a poorly designed new facility or space limitations more than circle": "Square reviewers repeatedly cite building and space problems: “While it is crowded and the building is very old,” and in follow‑up “Overall the new building has been a disaster.   "circle reports racialized bullying and POC students feeling unsafe and that incidents are inadequately addressed more than square": "Circle contains explicit, repeated allegations of race‑based mistreatment and unaddressed complaints: “If you are a person of color you will NOT feel safe here,” “I have reported them and nothing has happened,” and “countless acts of bullying and all St.Mary’s does is sweep it under the rug,” a pattern not present in square’s reviews.",
  "square reports frequent fights, extreme student stress, and a social climate where vulnerable students are at risk more than circle": "Square reviewers warn of a high‑stress, risky social environment: “riddled with kids who are extremely stressed out and at risk of succumbing to the pressures of the dark elements that lurk in the student body,” and “Fights are too frequent,” comments that emphasize violence and stress rather than the interpersonal/cliquey or racialized bullying themes reported in circle.",
  "circle highlights technology integration (1:1 iPad program) more than square": "Circle explicitly touts an iPad wireless learning system that “eliminates most text books” and reduces backpack weight, describing itself as “the first to have a I pad wireless learning system for high school students;” square’s reviews emphasize traditional AP/credit pathways and do not mention a school‑wide 1:1 device program."
}"]

["{
  "square describes concrete academic programs and measurable outcomes while circle does not": "Square lists specific advanced-course opportunities and outcomes (\"My daughter is taking 3 college level classes as a sophomore\", \"87% of the students have passed their WA state Math test\", \"many of the students...have passed exams and received college credit\"), whereas Circle offers only general praise about education effectiveness (\"the effectiveness of their education\") without program names or metrics.",
  "square reports targeted academic supports and remediation programs while circle does not": "Square names concrete supports for struggling students such as a \"homework center\" and a \"reading program\" that \"remediated young kids who failed their 7th grade reading tests and had them passing their 10th grade test\", but Circle gives no examples of formal remediation or support services.",
  "square describes explicit college-preparation emphasis and AP/college credit pathways more than circle": "Square repeatedly frames the school as preparing students for college from freshman year and cites AP/college options (\"preparing us for college from the first week of our freshman year\", \"AP classes, college preparation, support\", \"college level classes\"), while Circle simply states general educational effectiveness without mentioning college-prep programs or credit.",
  "square emphasizes strict discipline and absence of bullying while circle does not": "Square asserts a clear safety/discipline climate: \"the discipline is swift and strict\", \"the kids kind and thete is no bullying\", and contrasts this with a neighboring school's problems; Circle mentions caring teachers and listening administration but does not describe discipline, school safety, or bullying prevalence.",
  "square highlights broad extracurricular programs, school spirit and traditions more than circle": "Square references multiple extracurricular and cultural features (\"The music program is outstanding\", \"always something to get involved in and so much spirit as well as tradition\", \"labs in her science classes\"), whereas Circle contains no mention of extracurriculars, spirit, or traditions.",
  "circle signals controversy and unspecified concerns about the school while square emphasizes continuity and pride": "Circle explicitly says the school is \"Very ify and very controversial\" and \"There is many things concerning about this school\", indicating on-going concerns or controversies, while Square emphasizes a \"proud heritage\" that \"continues\" despite some changes.",
  "square situates the school in comparative context with other schools and external observers while circle does not": "Square compares this school favorably to at least one neighboring high school (\"I work at the neighboring high school...the bullying was shameful and rampant, and the cheating was out of control\"), using external comparison to support claims of quality; Circle offers no external comparisons.",
  "square gives specific staff/program examples and named practices while circle sticks to general praise": "Square cites concrete staff and program-level examples (\"Mr. Loupe is a great teacher\", \"IST program\", \"homework center\"), showing actionable practices and actors, whereas Circle only states that \"teachers and administration really seem to care and listen\" without naming programs, staff, or particular practices."

["{
  "square reports administrative cover up and unresponsiveness whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly states \"The Principal and Assistant Principal cover up any and all complaints\" and \"refused open discussion,\" indicating administrative obstruction and lack of accountability; Circle makes no such claim and instead notes staff accessibility with \"The teachers work with students hands on and are there if you have any questions or concerns.\"",
  "circle shows more hands-on teacher support and accessibility than square": "Circle says \"The teachers work with students hands on and are there if you have any questions or concerns,\" while Square complains \"I felt that I was never listen to my concerns and my sons education\" and says only \"There are a few good actual teachers here,\" indicating far less consistent teacher support.",
  "square reports poor IEP and special education responsiveness whereas circle does not": "Square calls out special education specifically: \"even the IEP instructors I felt that I was never listen to my concerns,\" showing failures in IEP support; Circle contains no mention of IEP or special education services.",

  "circle emphasizes a family atmosphere and explicit character education while square describes mistrust and disinterest in the school community": "Circle states \"teachers...pride themselves on teaching student character, work ethic, accountability, kindness\" and calls it \"a great family atmosphere,\" while Square speaks of \"disinterest and mistrust in this lack of education facility\" and warns parents about what they are \"inspiring them to become by sending them to a place like this.\"",
  "square reports stagnation or lack of improvement over time while circle reports early growth and recent achievements": "Square claims \"there obviously has been none [change] here in the time I have been away from this school,\" implying stagnation; Circle notes being present \"when the school opened up\" and cites rapid accomplishments like the band \"having won 2 State Titles in the short couple years of opening.\"",
  "circle reports a smaller student body and less student overwhelm whereas square does not note small size": "Circle explicitly says \"The student body isn't that large compared to other schools so students don't have to feel overwhelmed,\" indicating smaller enrollment and a less overwhelming environment; Square makes no claim about school size or reduced overwhelm."
}"]

["{
  "square describes AP and honors college preparatory programs while circle does not": "Square explicitly cites academic offerings and outcomes: “W-H and their honors and AP programs were an excellent preparation for the class work there” and notes admission to a “top-tier national university,” whereas Circle gives no information about course offerings or college preparation.",

  "circle provides structured college-prep programs and uneven favoritism toward high-achievers while square shows inconsistent academic quality and mixed support": "Circle repeatedly describes concrete college-prep offerings and preferential attention to high scorers (“college prep program is amazing… free overnight trips visiting out-of-state colleges… girls that scored well on the psat's and have higher averages get much more attention”), while Square contains contradictory academic reports—one reviewer says “academics were not at all up to snuff for a bright college-bound student,” others say staff “helped me through some of the hardest times”—indicating inconsistent academic quality/support rather than a coherent, resourced college-prep system.",
  "square reports lack of adult supervision and a chaotic in-school environment while circle attributes safety problems mainly to peer exclusion and neighborhood risks": "Square explicitly notes visiting the school and finding “a sense of chaos; of adults being there but not really paying attention to what was going on,” linking safety concerns to adult inattentiveness; Circle’s safety complaints center on peer dynamics and surrounding environment (e.g., “TMLA has an enormous bullying problem,” and concerns about homeless people near campus and assaults), not repeated claims that staff are inattentive in class.",
  "circle emphasizes well-maintained, attractive facilities (notably a distinguished library) more than square": "Circle repeatedly praises campus aesthetics and a distinctive library—“Mary Louis is the most beautiful school I have ever seen… Its library is just like stepping into Hogwarts… warm mahogany work tables”—whereas Square’s excerpts include no comparable descriptions of facilities.",
  "circle describes rigid, pressure-intensive academic policies that produce stress while square reports more individualized student engagement and personal improvement": "Circle cites concrete, high-pressure practices that increase stress—“tests count as 70% of your overall grade… staff make you choose your classes for next year in January… constant barraging from faculty to take honors and AP courses”—whereas Square highlights personal engagement and transformation for several students (“he put more effort into his work… the staff members of this school are amazing and helped me through some of the hardest times”).",
  "circle reports punitive administrative and financial practices (withheld privileges, forced summer school) that square does not mention": "Circle includes claims of punitive, policy-driven consequences tied to payments and performance—“Miss a tuition payment or walkathon donation and privileges are withheld,” and “this school still forced me to go to summer school because they didn't like my grades”—while Square contains no reports of financial penalties or similar institutional punishments.",
  "circle reports serious diversity, equity, and inclusion failures (racism, exclusion of students of color and LGBTQ+ students) while square does not": "Multiple Circle reviewers allege exclusionary and racist dynamics and warn against sending students of color or LGBTQ+ students (“I would not recommend this school for students of color nor LGBTQ+ students… Racist bullies… if she is not the Caucasian, christian, rich girl”), whereas Square’s excerpts do not raise diversity, race, or LGBTQ+ inclusion as issues.",
  "circle contains concurrent reports of strong sisterhood and entrenched social stratification/cliques, whereas square mostly emphasizes individual staff relationships and student turnaround stories": "Circle includes both claims that single-gender education creates a sisterhood (“The idea of all girls fosters the belief that women can be leaders… I've found life long friends”) and counterclaims about cliques and luxury-based social exclusion (“if you dont own a Louis Vuitton bag… you are considered garbage… The amount of cliques there are is obsurd”), while Square’s comments focus primarily on individual positive staff interactions and personal success narratives (naming staff and stating “it was the best school I had ever been to”) rather than school-wide social stratification."
}"]

["{
  "circle has substantially stronger advanced academic programs, college-prep outcomes, and external recognition than square": "Circle repeatedly cites advanced coursework and outcomes—'AP American History and AP Composition', 'IB Diploma', 'college credit', 'earned a scholarship'—and external rankings ('recognized by U.S. News and World Report and Newsweek', 'ranked #2 in the State') whereas Square contains no mention of AP/IB programs, college-credit pathways, scholarships, or national rankings.",
  "circle offers a broader set of extracurricular and enrichment opportunities than square": "Circle lists 'a large selection of clubs, activities and sports', 'numerous student organizations', 'Intersession', and 'numerous athletic teams', while Square focuses almost exclusively on disciplinary and classroom-control problems and gives no examples of organized enrichment programming.",
  "circle identifies curricular resource gaps and an excessive emphasis on athletics more than square": "Circle specifically notes 'too much emphasis placed upon athletics' and calls for 'more resources to hiring superior math and science teachers' and 'offer IB computer science', criticisms absent from Square which centers on behavior and supervision issues rather than curricular balance or STEM staffing.",
  "square reports frequent safety incidents and pervasive student misbehavior with examples more than circle": "Square details acute behavior problems: 'Fights last week three(3) in one day', 'really bad students...still continue to hurt others', and 'PHHS is really out of control', while Circle's critiques focus mostly on programmatic or isolated personal experiences rather than ongoing, school-wide violent incidents.",
  "square describes ineffective discipline policies and lack of meaningful consequences more than circle": "Square complains that 'really bad students are given a mild ISS and still continue to hurt others' and notes a 'Lack of OSS (out of school suspensions)', demonstrating weak enforcement; Circle, by contrast, notes 'administration provides more consistent discipline' and the main administrative critique is policy decisions (e.g., eliminating Add/Drop) rather than wholesale lack of enforcement.",
  "square reports poor classroom-level supervision by substitutes and teacher-coverage problems more than circle": "Square gives concrete examples of substitute teachers 'reading' and 'do not monitor the students' while 'students completed a very bad activity...the substitute did not catch', a classroom-level supervision failure not described in Circle.",
  "square shows more parental activism and public complaining about administration responsiveness than circle": "Square emphasizes parents 'in an up`roar', direct attempts to contact leadership ('Sent an email to the superintendent...He never returned my email or call') and calls for leadership replacement, while Circle contains mostly parent/student endorsements and only measured administrative criticism (policy choices, counseling improvements) rather than the same level of organized public grievance."
}"]

  "square reports superior facilities, dining options, and flexible lunch policy more than circle": "Square lists campus amenities and policies: \"off campus lunch is great, the principals are friendly, the cafeteria and cafe with its many varieties of cusine and beverages...the building itself is stunning\" and \"we can sit anywhere we want during lunch,\" whereas Circle only references the track fence (vandalism) and gives no positive facility or dining details.",
  "square reports large school size and faster pace requiring adjustment more than circle": "Square describes scale and the adjustment it requires: \"Union is a very big district with very big schools...it was a challenge at first to adjust to the higher curriculum, pace and size of Union,\" a structural attribute of the school not mentioned in Circle.",
  "circle reports campus hostility or rival vandalism incidents more than square": "Circle describes a vandalism/hostility incident on campus: \"on the fench of the school's track it spelled out SCHS ( another local high school) ******* and I couldn't tolerate with that,\" a concrete campus-safety/behavior issue not referenced in Square.",
  "square reports strong school spirit and student support networks more than circle": "Square emphasizes communal student support and spirit: \"School spirit is huge...You can see how much students want to support one another, and sports...The students are encouraged and supported!\" Circle gives no comparable evidence of broad school spirit or organized peer support.",
  "circle reports direct parental statements of children thriving despite administrative shortcomings more than square": "Circle provides explicit parental outcome claims tied to a student's wellbeing despite management problems: \"Duchesne is an awesome school and my child has thrived there. ["{
  "square shows more organized, responsive communication between administration, teachers, students and parents than circle": "Square states explicitly “very organized, good communication between administration, teachers, students and parents” and praises staff for being “Always in the good mood to provided fast and reasonable solution to your concerning,” whereas Circle repeatedly reports “Poor communication between the school and parents” and that “As a parent trying to communicate with the school about any issue is simply ridiculous.”",
  "square exhibits stronger leadership and higher parental support/involvement than circle": "Square praises leadership and family engagement: “It's not perfect, but it has strong leadership, mostly great teachers and an extraordinary level of parental support and involvement,” while Circle describes failing leadership and calls for removal of leaders: “All school staff in a leadership role need to be removed” despite noting active parents and community support.",
  "circle exhibits a hostile bullying and punitive school climate (including staff-perpetrated bullying) whereas square does not": "Circle documents bullying by staff and inadequate response: “The bullying has taken place by teachers not students,” “The administration at the H.S. and Middle school is not good...are bullies them selves,” and describes the school using a “‘bullying button’ ...a mechanism to protect the school - not the students.” Square contains no complaints about bullying and instead emphasizes a positive school climate.",
  "square provides stronger advanced academic programs and better college-prep outcomes than circle": "Square lists concrete advanced offerings and outcomes: students “were part of the magnet program, participated in sports and took AP classes” and “There is a place for AP students aiming for elite universities.” Circle reports the opposite: “There is not enough ap classes,” “Students are poorly prepared for college,” and “Their test scores are awful.”",
  "circle reports widespread staff underperformance, perceived overpayment, and lack of accountability more than square": "Circle includes accusations that many staff “overpaid teachers that don't do their job, overpaid principals that don't do their jobs - they will ignore you, take no accountability,” and calls for mass staff removal; square, by contrast, praises teachers as “so professional and dedicated.”",
  "circle reports limited elective and language offerings while square reports a broader set of extracurricular and program options (magnet, athletics, AP)": "Circle notes electives need beefing up and that “Currently they only offer spanish” and “There is not enough class options,” whereas Square highlights multiple pathways: “magnet program...participated in sports and took AP classes” and praises “Athletics, Academics, and encouragement.”",
  "circle highlights a strong music program and new facilities more than square": "Circle specifically says “They have a very strong music program and new facilities,” an item not mentioned in Square, which emphasizes athletics, magnet and academics instead.",
  "circle fails to foster diversity and inclusion while square emphasizes a diverse student body and inclusive pathways": "Circle states bluntly “they do not foster or address diversity at all - if your child is different in any way - they will do nothing” and warns students must “have the right looks,” whereas Square claims “The student body is diverse in every way” and that there is “a place for AP students...and everything in between.”",
  "circle relies more on punitive responses and police involvement for conflicts than square": "Circle criticizes the principal for being “arrogant and condescending” and “rather than handling conflicts himself is too quick to police,” while Square describes administrators as responsive and solving concerns quickly without mention of punitive policing."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports pervasive, severe student bullying and administrative failure to address it whereas square describes a kind student community and supportive staff": "Circle states: \"Was bullied from kindergarten all the way up until my senior year and teachers nor principal or vice principal did anything to stop it\" and \"Students would tell me to self harm and kill myself. Nothing was done about it.\" Square, by contrast, says \"All of my classmates are good people who have treated me with so much kindness\" and \"The teachers always make an effort to get to know their students,\" showing a safer, more supportive student-staff climate in square reviews.",

["{
  "square reports more staff sexual misconduct and other inappropriate touching incidents than circle": "Square explicitly alleges multiple sexual-misconduct incidents: “Mr. Story a track coach has been observed by parents inappropriately putting his hands on female students,” “A 6 grade girl was fondled by an 8th grader on the bus,” and “a teacher kissed a 10th grade girl,” whereas Circle contains no reports of abuse or safety incidents.",

["{
  "circle attributes school failure to local poverty and community separation more than square": "Circle explicitly links poor outcomes to economics and community division: “Its success is hampered because of the poverty level and general low economics of the area” and “one of the biggest issues ... is the seperation of the community,” while Square contains no sustained claim that local poverty or community fragmentation is the primary structural cause of problems.",
  "square exhibits governance instability and board mismanagement more than circle": "Square states governance/leadership problems as central: “administration has changed several times… they have had three different principals alone!” and “Board of directors keep unworthy teachers to fill the void and do not manage complaints / termination,” claims that are absent in Circle (which never documents frequent principal turnover or explicit board failure).",

  "square reports inadequate support for students with disabilities requiring parental advocacy more than circle": "Square includes direct claims about poor treatment of students with disabilities and the need for parental fight: “poor treatment of children that may have a disability( minor /major)” and “My mother had to fight tooth and nail for me to get the proper education,” whereas Circle does not raise disabilities or required parental advocacy as a school-level problem.",
  "circle emphasizes a strong athletic program and community backing more than square": "Circle contains a positive depiction of athletics and local support: “Turner not only offers the some of the highest academic standards in the state but also has the best athletic program… high standards of leadership in a community who entirely supports there school,” language that presents athletics as a community-strength not mirrored in Square.",
  "square reports favoritism toward athletes that disadvantages non-athletes more than circle": "Square accuses the school of privileging athletes over other students: “They definitely favored athletes and more intelligent people than people who were not so ‘gifted’,” framing athletics as a source of unequal treatment, a claim Circle frames more as program prestige than favoritism.",
  "square reports a district-wide scarcity of advanced course offerings more than circle": "Square repeatedly emphasizes limited advanced classes as a systemic offering problem: “I don't know what the other reviewers are talking about when it comes to advanced courses. There aren't many offered at all,” whereas Circle’s complaints focus on individual students being denied harder classes through labeling rather than an overall paucity of advanced offerings.",
  "circle attributes lack of access to advanced classes to teacher labeling and exclusion of non-gifted students more than square": "Circle blames educators' perceptions for denying access: “because they didn't consider me one of the smart kids or gifted kids, I felt I was deprived of… the harder classes” and “My teachers labeled me and acted as if I wouldn't amount to anything,” framing exclusion as teacher/advising behavior rather than sole scarcity of courses.",
  "circle shows multigenerational alumni involvement and expressed ongoing pride/support more than square": "Circle contains multigenerational ties and explicit alumni support: “I graduated from Turner County in 1978. My oldest daughter graduated in 1993. I have a grandson in 1st grade… I am proud to be a Turner alumni and will continue to offer my support,” whereas Square includes a graduate voice but no sustained multigenerational pride or continued institutional backing."
}"]

["{
  "square reports stronger special education support and IEP compliance than circle": "Square includes multiple detailed accounts of special education services: “He was put right into an IEP and they have been doing a wonderful job at following what it says” and mentions an “excellent special education teacher” and social worker Mitch Kilgore, whereas Circle makes no comparable claims about IEP implementation or sustained special-education supports.",
  "circle reports more bullying, racism, and weak enforcement of discipline than square": "Circle explicitly alleges failures of discipline and discrimination: “The School Does Not Enforce The Bullying Policy … There Is So Much Racisim,” while Square asserts the opposite climate: “Bullying really just didn't exist.”",
  "square reports broader extracurricular opportunities and less exclusion from teams than circle": "Square emphasizes wide access to activities and no cuts: “so many opportunities to play sports, no getting cut from the team” and students mixing across activities (“star of the soccer team would also be the lead of the musical”), whereas Circle repeatedly asks for “more extra activities besides sports” and critiques a sports/popularity focus.",

["{

  "circle shows preferential treatment for athletes resulting in unequal support for non‑athletes more than square": "Circle reports a clear split in support: the son who played sports “had an amazing guidance counselor, & a great vice principal” and received athletic scholarships, while the high‑achieving daughter “carries a 4.3 gpa…her guidance counselor…will not respond” and the vice principal was “uncaring,” and the reviewer states “I truly believe athletes get preferential treatment.” Square does not report athlete favoritism.",

  "circle reports lower parent attendance and engagement at conferences more than square": "Circle includes a direct parental concern: “Very disappointed in the turn out on the parents side as to not showing up for conferences,” indicating a noted lack of parent participation; square contains no mention of parent conference turnout or similar parental disengagement.",
  "circle emphasizes broad college preparatory coursework and claims near‑universal college access more than square": "Circle repeatedly asserts academic breadth and college readiness: “They teach more, in less time, and go into more depth than many college classes,” “These students graduate with an education that grants them entrance to ANY school they might want to attend,” and praises a “tremendous selection of coursework that will help anyone go to college of choice.” Square mentions AP classes and smoother college transition but does not assert universal college access.",
  "square highlights pronounced strength in arts and literature curriculum and in AP science outcomes more than circle": "Square states explicit program strengths: “top notch arts education--band, choir, fine arts,” “unopposed literature and rhetoric education,” and that “natural sciences are also well developed…based on AP scores and pass rates,” showing concrete program-level strengths not present in circle.",

["{

  "circle shows higher measurable academic outcomes and advanced course opportunities than square": "Circle claims measurable academic results and advanced offerings: 'turning out as many national merit scholarship semi-finalists' and 'taking great, advanced classes,' while Square only refers to passing with homework and help and mentions no honors/AP/merit achievements.",
  "circle exhibits more systemic administrative bureaucracy and politics affecting academics than square": "Circle repeatedly reports administrative obstacles and internal politics that affect academics: 'Bureaucratic administration,' 'administration gets annoyed when you try to test out,' and 'politics that the teachers and administration would play,' whereas Square does not describe institutional politics or testing/placement obstruction.",
  "circle has worse staff communication responsiveness and a more adversarial teacher-student climate than square": "Circle documents unanswered parent outreach and adversarial teacher behavior: 'three emails went unanswered by the teacher,' 'Most of the teachers... see their role as adversarial, spend a lot of time yelling at kids,' and a principal who 'seems to hide in his office,' while Square states 'I had great relations with all the teachers' and 'The environment within the classrooms was very open and welcoming.'",
  "circle reports special education accommodation failures and confusing grading mechanics whereas square does not": "Circle includes a parent account of special education failure tied to grading mechanics: 'as a parent of a special ed student I was appalled... my child couldn't pass a class... taking into account the 80% mastery weighting... my child could have passed,' indicating accommodation and grading-system problems; Square contains no discussion of special education provision.",
  "circle reports facility and scheduling strains such as overcrowded lunches more than square": "Circle describes concrete facility/scheduling strain: 'There are 2 half-hour lunch periods for the entire school of 1500 kids.   "square reports a harmful emergency contact policy blocking family communication during a student mental health crisis whereas circle does not": "Square recounts a specific crisis incident: 'my little brother has depression and tried to call me for help while at school, and they denied me from talking to him because i didnt have permission from his mother,' showing a rigid permission policy that prevented family contact during a mental-health episode; Circle contains no comparable crisis-response example.",
  "square reports resource limitations tied to serving a poor community more than circle": "Square explicitly links limited resources to poverty: 'this school was below standard in resources we could obtain from being in a poor community,' whereas Circle frames its context as an 'educated community' with many students going to four-year colleges and cites competitive outcomes.",
  "circle emphasizes notable extracurricular breadth and daily strong music program more than square": "Circle praises extracurriculars and daily music participation: 'The extracurriculum is amazing and my daughter just loves it' and 'performing in an excellent band program every day,' while Square does not describe robust extracurricular programs."

["{
  "circle reports administrative corruption and program cuts while square does not": "Circle explicitly alleges governance problems and concrete consequences: “after recent budget cuts, great teachers have been lost,” “the budget allocation system is very corrupt,” and “causing program cuts in necessary technology courses,” plus “Some school departments receive greater support from administration than others.” Square contains no claims of corrupt allocation or targeted program cuts.",
  "circle reports loss of teachers and lowered staff morale while square emphasizes continued teacher quality and positive experiences": "Circle says “great teachers have been lost” and the author is “dishearten[ed]” by administrative actions, linking leadership to staff attrition; square repeatedly affirms teacher quality and past positive experiences: “the teachers I went to high school here and enjoyed my time there,” “we both had wonderful experiences,” and “including the teachers.”",
  "square describes explicit college preparatory programming and college credit opportunities while circle does not": "Square highlights programmatic college readiness: “set up like a mini college campus,” “classes also prepared us for college,” and “some students get college credit for certain courses,” whereas Circle focuses on budget/program cuts and mentions no college-preparatory offerings or dual‑credit opportunities.",
  "square documents strong community participation, neighborhood reputation, and alumni/family continuity while circle does not": "Square emphasizes community and continuity: “we love all the participation and community activities,” “this school and neighborhood is not only the best in Lake Charles,” “My kids really enjoy it,” and family ties: “my Mother was a substitute teacher there before I attended,” indicating broad parent/alumni/community engagement that Circle does not describe.",
  "square notes a specific facilities cleanliness concern that circle does not mention": "Square admits one concrete facilities issue: “The only thing this school doesn't offer is a absolute clean environment,” while Circle makes no mention of physical plant or cleanliness problems."
}"]

["{
  "square highlights elite college placements and distinguished top students more than circle": "Square directly cites high-end matriculations and class-tops: “My classes valedictorian attended Duke and there were multiple students who went Ivy league,” and frames the school as sending “kids to some of the best schools in the county,” whereas Circle describes general academic challenge but gives no evidence of elite college outcomes.",
  "circle reports explicit on-campus substance use incidents (students smoking in bathrooms) more than square": "Circle names a specific, ongoing substance-use location: “people smoke in the bathrooms.. it's nasty,” an incident-level safety concern not described in Square.",
  "circle documents concrete daily operational policies and timings more than square": "Circle lists specific logistics and policies: “they give plenty of time to get to your classes [5-6 minutes], enough time to eat [25 minutes],” and allowances like “students are allowed to have their phones out in the circle and during lunch” and “most teachers allow students to chew gum too,” details Square does not provide.",
  "square emphasizes strong athletics tradition and visible school spirit more than circle": "Square repeatedly foregrounds team tradition and fan culture — “The Athletics have a great tradition,” “GO SPARTANS!!”, and “football games are amazing…,” presenting school spirit as a defining feature, far more prominent than in Circle.",
  "circle reports targeted bullying tied to socioeconomic appearance and resulting emotional harm more than square": "Circle gives a concrete example of bullying with emotional impact: “when you see your grandaughter come home in tears… the bullying that goes on cause the child maybe doesn't wear expensive clothes or looks a little different,” whereas Square mentions cliques and occasional fights but not this kind of described targeted emotional harm.",
  "square reports systemic administrative neglect of struggling students and poor conflict resolution more than circle": "Square accuses staff/administration of failing students and mishandling conflict: “They are more focused on behavior of students then there grades and don't help kids when they fall behind… They treat all the students like cattle and encouraging violence and fighting by not properly addressing issues,” claims not present in Circle's account of staff behavior.",
  "circle emphasizes caring, student-focused staff practices that balance grades and enjoyment more than square": "Circle stresses that “the teachers care about your grades, but the staff also cares about you having a good time,” and notes staff efforts to make school enjoyable, including permissive in-school phone/gum policies and caring coaches/athletic trainer—portrayals of active student-centered practice less evident in Square.",
  "square reports greater socioeconomic and population diversity while circle reports lack of cultural/background diversity": "Square explicitly states greater socioeconomic diversity and a broad population: “Tabor is more diverse in the socioeconomic category” and “Great teachers and administration with a very diverse population,” whereas Circle states an “extreme lack of diversity in background, culture, and beliefs.”",
  "circle highlights on-site athletic medical/support presence and caring coaches more than square": "Circle specifically praises athletic staff and medical support: “the coaches are caring especially when an athlete gets hurt and the athletic trainer is very good at what she does,” a concrete resource that Square does not mention despite talking about athletics more generally."
}"]

["{
  "square offers a broader range of electives, advanced courses, and academic tracks than circle": "Square lists many specialized offerings and pathways — e.g., “unique electives (Computer Science, Robotics, Business Management, Culinary Arts, Pre-Med, Law, Dance, Studio Art, Theatre, etc.),” “STEM Academy,” and “more AP classes than your typical NYC public high school.” Circle mentions Dual Enrollment and some Honors/AP students but lacks the same catalogue of varied electives and tracks (circle mainly notes “Dual Enrollment” and that “my 2 kids ... are both in Honors and AP classes”).",
  "square provides explicit transition and ongoing student supports that circle does not describe": "Square describes a one‑week Summer Bridge program for incoming freshmen (“One fourth of the incoming class (Class of 2017) attended Dewey's Summer Bridge program”), tutors, after‑school support and mental health resources (“The school pays attention to its students... provides many mental health resources... tutors who are really helpful”). Circle contains no comparable description of structured transition programs or schoolwide student support offerings.",
  "square shows more consistent teacher engagement and proactive parent communication than circle": "Square repeatedly notes attentive, proactive staff — “the teachers really care... the teachers even call the house to remind the parents of upcoming exams,” and “teachers are very encouraging and provide help whenever needed.” Circle contains direct complaints about instructional inattention: “the teachers do not teach you really because they are on their cell phones or on the internent.”",
  "circle reports more student violence, bullying, and racial harassment and less evidence of inclusive cultural integration than square": "Circle explicitly reports unsafe behavior and harassment: “the students want to fight you for no reason,” “there are also alot of racial comments,” and “kids do innapropiate things everywhere.” Square, by contrast, emphasizes safety, inclusion and international diversity (“Dewey is both safe and cares for its students,” “I've seen students from Tibet and Mongolia here”), indicating stronger cultural representation and fewer reported safety incidents.",
  "circle experiences overcrowding and operational strain on facilities and transportation more than square": "Circle documents crowding and capacity problems: “the lunch room line is horrible and there are never any room to sit,” “the buses are crowded,” and someone states the school is “well over capacity for students.” Square contains no reporting of cafeteria or bus overcrowding or overcapacity issues.",
  "circle enforces restrictive restroom and tardy policies that produce punitive detentions whereas square reports no such policy": "Circle repeatedly describes locked bathrooms during class and punitive tardy consequences: “students cannot use the restroom during class... The bathrooms are all locked during class time... If you get three tardies you get detention,” and parents report unsuccessful appeals. Square contains no mention of restrictive restroom passes or routine detentions for such issues.",
  "circle demonstrates problematic disciplinary procedures and confidentiality breaches compared with square’s more supportive handling": "Circle recounts a disciplinary meeting mishandled in a way that exposed a witness and influenced the outcome: “they went with what one side said because the person brought in a parent... they questioned their witness with the door open so I could hear everything they said.” Square emphasizes caring staff who call families and support students rather than describing such procedural failures."
}"]

["{
  "square shows stronger college preparation and documented postsecondary outcomes than circle": "Square repeatedly cites measurable college outcomes and advanced coursework—e.g., “My senior is 8 for 8 for college acceptances,” “Both went to highly ranked colleges… earned advanced degrees from Columbia and Drexel,” and lists “AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Bio.” Circle describes weaker preparation and program gaps: “Lacking in a lot of programs that could be beneficial… the school could use more funding and better teachers.”",
  "square provides broader extracurricular and elective options and higher participation than circle": "Square emphasizes many clubs and activities and high participation: “students are able to participate in a number of different clubs and extracurricular activities,” “Almost all students participate in extra-curricular activities,” and mentions a “robotics club.” Circle, by contrast, notes program scarcity: “Lacking in a lot of programs that could be beneficial….”",
  "square emphasizes small size and individualized teacher attention more than circle": "Square repeatedly highlights small classes and personal attention: “With less than 100 students per graduating class, PHS offers personalized attention,” “Because of the small size… students are able to get individual attention from their teachers.” Circle does not describe small-class individualized support and instead focuses on systemic deficits.",
  "circle reports more ongoing incidents of homophobia, racism, and ineffective institutional response than square": "Circle explicitly states discriminatory incidents and lack of mitigation: “I’ve been in a situation with a lot of homophobia and racism, the school does nothing to prevent this,” and notes only minimal interventions “some/barely any videos shown….” Square contains no comparable reports of racial or homophobic incidents.",
  "circle highlights funding and teacher-quality shortfalls more than square": "Circle calls out resource and staffing problems directly: “the school could use more funding and better teachers throughout,” and says the school is “lacking in a lot of programs.” Square’s reviews focus on program offerings and staff engagement rather than systemic underfunding.",
  "square presents stronger multigenerational alumni engagement and community pride than circle": "Square includes multiple alumni and family success narratives and long-term community ties: “As a former graduate and parent… Both went to highly ranked colleges,” “6 of my siblings attend Palmyra… four of my nieces and nephews,” and “I'm a Palmyra Alumna.” Circle mentions long residency (“I have lived in Cleveland for 34 years”) but provides far fewer examples of generational academic success or alumni outcomes."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports low academic rigor and grade inflation more than square": "Circle states exams are \"open book, open Internet\" and \"hands out As like candy,\" adding that exams are \"so simple\" they resemble 7th grade work; square contains mixed statements about academic preparation (some say \"well prepared for College,\" others say \"Not good place for young people to develop character or life skills\") rather than the consistent claim of systemic grade inflation and permissive testing policies.",
  "circle describes frequent teacher turnover disrupting a single course more than square": "Circle gives a concrete example of classroom continuity loss: \"I had three different math teachers for the same math class,\" emphasizing turnover's direct impact on one course; square mentions turnover broadly but not the same focused, single-course continuity example.",
  "square reports district and leadership turnover and mass staff exits more than circle": "Square explicitly mentions administrative departures and a \"mass exodus\" (\"fired the principal of Salem... buried in an e-mail... mass exodus\" and \"Of the five teachers my oldest has had, three have already left or been let go\"), pointing to district-level churn and leadership change that circle does not describe.",
  "square documents ongoing bullying and safety problems that are ignored by staff more than circle": "Square details numerous safety incidents and ignored reports — \"countless reports of students bullying kids and the principal pushes it to the side,\" a slur caught on camera but dismissed, and repeated food-throwing by students that administrators failed to stop — whereas circle contains no reports of bullying or safety concerns.",
  "square reports active administrative misconduct and punitive mishandling of students more than circle": "Square accuses a named administrator of lying and harming students' outcomes (\"Catherine Trevathan is not fit... she lied to my whole family... she belittled me, told me I was nothing and refused to give me my diploma\"), describing punitive, erroneous discipline and withholding of diplomas — allegations absent from circle.",
  "square reports poor and opaque communication from district/staff more than circle": "Square gives multiple examples of communication failures: teachers fired without notice told to parents later by students, principal firing \"buried in an e-mail newsletter,\" and inconsistent notifications (\"send a district wide text to say a bus is late, but can’t notify anyone when staff leaves\"), while circle does not discuss communication practices.",
  "square reports favoritism toward athletes and majority-group students and potential discrimination more than circle": "Square describes perceptions of selective enforcement and bias: \"Kids that do drugs and are in sports....completely overlooked\" and \"If you are a straight, white student who is good at sports - you may enjoy it,\" plus incidents involving \"popular white male athletes\" throwing food — themes not present in circle.",
  "square presents highly mixed, polarized user outcomes while circle presents a consistent academic complaint": "Square juxtaposes glowing parental testimonials (\"My family had a great experience... well prepared for College\") with severe complaints about safety, administration, and student welfare, producing a polarized set of experiences; circle is uniformly focused on the single consistent issue of weak academic rigor and readiness."
}"]

  "circle documents explicit honors/AP and college credit course access for gifted students more than square": "Circle includes concrete statements about advanced coursework: \"Parkway offers honors and AP courses and both my children ... have already been able to take college level courses and receive college credits,\" whereas Square praises getting on track academically and college admissions but gives no specific claims about AP/honors or college-credit coursework.",

["{

  "circle reports financial and program mismanagement (including a failed laptop program) more than square": "Circle explicitly claims “Total inability to properly manage or spend money appropriately” and that “The laptop program is completely worthless due to it being run with people very unfamiliar,” whereas Square contains no comparable complaints about district finances or major program rollouts.",
  "circle reports grade-based neglect of lower-performing students more than square": "Circle states “Students with lower GPAs are shafted and pushed along without learning anything” and questions workload imbalance between high- and low-GPA students, a specific claim of GPA-based neglect not present in Square.",
  "square reports program-based elitism and social division (IB versus general population) more than circle": "Square repeatedly calls out IB as creating division and elitism—“IB Program is an elitist program that breeds the students to hate traditional program students” and notes minority students feeling pressure in IB—whereas Circle’s divisions are framed around leadership/management or GPA, not magnet-program social stratification.",
  "square emphasizes formal specialized programs and measurable student outcomes more than circle": "Square lists multiple formal programs and concrete outcomes—“IB Program,” “Health academy,” “Air Force JR ROTC,” “8 National Merit Scholarship winners,” and “Students were awarded more scholarships… $16 MILLION dollars!”—while Circle mentions college readiness and rigorous curriculum but provides no comparable program inventory or quantified outcomes.",
  "square documents explicit student-support policies and case-level accommodations more than circle": "Square gives examples of responsive practices: staff “worked with us through one child going through many missed days due to chronic illness” via emails and phone, and deans actively engage parents; Circle instead highlights managerial abuse and curricular fragmentation with little evidence of system-level support.",
  "circle frames teacher competence as the primary saving factor more than square": "Circle repeatedly asserts teachers are the redeeming quality—“If it were not for the relative competence of the teachers, there would be no redeeming qualities to this school” and “The teachers are top notch”—positioning teacher quality as the main corrective to other school failings; Square praises teachers but pairs that praise with institutional programs and outcomes rather than framing teachers as the sole savior.",
  "circle reports a recent, abrupt decline since 2015-2016 while square frames past problems as historical and emphasizes current improvement": "Circle says “None of the above referenced difficulties existed prior to the 2015-2016 academic year which until then was an outstanding school,” implying a sharp recent downturn; Square notes critics citing events “over 20 yrs ago” and concentrates on the school’s current strengths and improvements.",
  "square reports family logistical burdens around transportation more than circle": "Square includes a parent-level logistical complaint—“The only draw back is I end up driving them to school early, picking up late so riding the bus doesn't happen often”—a concrete operational/family-burden detail absent from Circle."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports stronger community integration and consistently high athletics and academic program quality than square": "Circle states a “near-perfect mix of a small town, personal feel and state-quality learning and athletics,” and concludes “ROCORI is a great school for local kids to experience a quality education,” whereas Square contains scattered praise for specific programs (e.g. “this afternoon, I attended the Drama Club's performance of Aida.   "circle reports resolved financial and mass-retirement staffing instability while square describes ongoing staffing turnover and a need for new hires": "Circle explicitly says “The previous financial woes and mass retirements issues have been solved and are largely gone,” indicating recovered stability; Square repeatedly urges “let's get in some new blood” and that “some of the teachers need to be updated,” implying unresolved staffing quality/turnover issues.",
  "circle describes a safer, better-managed bullying and disciplinary climate than square": "Circle asserts bullying is “a non-issue (very rarely do I see physical violence... and verbal bullying is similarly rare), yet the school still makes a large effort to prevent it,” and urges consequences for bullies; Square, however, reports “There are bullies,” “Teachers don't help the students when they are in need,” and multiple reviewers say the school “is great at leaving children behind,” signaling more frequent bullying and weaker responses.",
  "square shows more widespread evidence of outdated teaching methods and inconsistent teacher effectiveness than circle": "Square repeatedly criticizes instruction as “techniques are SO outdated,” “they barely teach and give out confusing packets,” and “few teachers that do extremely well,” indicating pervasive and inconsistent instructional quality, while Circle’s only instructional gripe is “inconsistent homework levels and grading,” with overall praise that the school “does a great job of preparing students for post secondary success.”",
  "square reports poorer support for struggling and special education students compared with circle": "Square states “Teachers are giving up on the lower end students,” and that staff need to “learn the meaning of the term 'special needs'… They are in the dark,” whereas Circle does not describe systemic failures supporting struggling learners and instead highlights post-secondary preparation.",
  "square reports adversarial staff–parent relations and low parent engagement while circle reports accountable staff": "Square documents an “us vs. them attitude with the parents,” notes parent withdrawal and low conference turnout (“the entire school might have 30 parents show up”), and that reviewers moved their children away; Circle emphasizes staff responsibility with statements like “teachers and staff take responsibility and change!” suggesting more constructive staff–community relations.",
  "square reports facility and cosmetic neglect and calls for an extreme overhaul while circle does not raise facility concerns": "Square explicitly demands “an extreme overhaul cosmetically and academically,” indicating visible facility/appearance concerns, whereas Circle makes no mention of building condition or cosmetic issues.",
  "circle reports stronger post‑secondary preparation outcomes than square": "Circle asserts “ROCORI does a great job of preparing students for post secondary success,” while Square includes warnings that students are unlikely to reach college readiness in places (“I can't recommend you'll go to college with their teaching abilities”) despite some conflicting positive comments."
}"]
